A genuine, active runtime enforcement mechanism is materially stronger evidence of effective control than a documented policy alone, and this distinction, between a written rule and an actively enforced one, should be a specific point of examination when assessing an organization's agent governance claims.

terms.example: An agent's payment attempt checked against amount and counterparty policy at call time.
terms.definition: Evaluating each attempted action against policy at the moment it is attempted, rather than trusting a role granted in advance. It is enforcement, not documentation: the policy engine sits in the execution path and can say no.

lenses.body: A legal shortcut where following an officially recognized standard is automatically assumed to mean you met the underlying legal requirement, which flips who has to prove what: someone challenging you now has to prove you did not actually follow the standard.

Document explicit adherence to the specific applicable harmonised standard as part of your technical documentation, since this presumption only applies where genuine, demonstrable adherence exists, not merely a general claim of following best practices.

A meaningful compliance strategy advantage worth pursuing wherever a relevant harmonised standard exists; following the standard, rather than developing a custom compliance approach, shifts the evidentiary burden favorably and represents the lower-risk, lower-cost compliance path in most cases.

It shifts the burden of proof: a challenger must show the standard was not followed or does not cover the case, rather than the deployer proving compliance from scratch; leverage available harmonised standards to obtain this presumption wherever applicable, since it substantially reduces the evidentiary burden compared to demonstrating compliance from first principles.

terms.origin: EU product-safety law doctrine.
terms.example: Citing conformity with a harmonised standard as the front-line answer to an enforcement inquiry.
terms.definition: The legal assumption that following a cited standard satisfies the underlying regulatory requirement. It shifts the burden of proof: a challenger must show the standard was not followed or does not cover the case, rather than the deployer proving compliance from scratch.

lenses.body: A specific number that limits how much any single piece of personal information is allowed to influence what an AI model produces, used in a mathematical privacy protection method. If a company says their system is privacy-protecting this way but will not give you the actual number, that claim cannot really be checked or trusted.

The number is the claim: a "differentially private" system quoted without an epsilon value is an unevidenced assertion. Require the specific epsilon value whenever a vendor or internal team claims differential privacy protection, since the claim is genuinely meaningless and unverifiable without this specific parameter disclosed.

A differential privacy claim without a disclosed and justified epsilon value should be treated as an unsubstantiated assertion rather than verified evidence of privacy protection, since the strength of the actual privacy guarantee is entirely determined by this specific numeric parameter.

The choice of epsilon involves a genuine and often underexplained tradeoff between privacy protection strength and resulting model utility, and this tradeoff, along with its justification for a specific chosen value, deserves explicit reporting whenever differential privacy is claimed in published work.

terms.origin: Differential privacy literature, Dwork et al., 2006.
terms.example: A vendor asked to state the epsilon behind its privacy-preserving analytics claim.
terms.definition: The parameter, epsilon, bounding how much any single record can influence a model's output under differential privacy. The number is the claim: a "differentially private" system quoted without an epsilon value is an unevidenced assertion.

lenses.body: A person's right to have their personal information deleted. With AI, this gets tricky because deleting the original data record does not automatically remove its influence from everywhere: a model that already learned from that information may still carry traces of it inside its learned settings, even after the original record is gone.

Build and test deletion verification procedures that specifically check for residual presence in derived systems, vector stores, caches, and, where feasible, assess whether trained model behavior still reflects deleted data; a deletion audit that only checks the primary data store will miss real, technically genuine incompleteness.

Confirm your organization's deletion process for erasure requests actually addresses derived data, embeddings, cached copies, model training influence, not just the original database record; a deletion process that stops at the source record while leaving derivatives intact is technically incomplete regardless of good intentions.

Erasure that stops before the embedding store is incomplete by design; require deletion verification to specifically cover derived artifacts, embeddings, cached representations, trained model influence, not just the original source record, since technical completeness of erasure genuinely requires addressing all of these, not only the most visible one.

terms.origin: GDPR Article 17.
terms.example: A deletion workflow that removes the source record and the embeddings generated from it.
terms.definition: An individual's right to have their personal data deleted. In AI systems the practical question is where deletion stops: source rows can be removed while derived embeddings and trained weights still carry the influence, and erasure that stops before the embedding store is incomplete by design.

lenses.body: A detailed ingredient list of every software component and dependency actually built into a piece of software. It tells you which pieces of code are inside a product, but it does not tell you anything about what data was actually used to train the AI model that also happens to be part of that product.

It answers component provenance, not data licensing: an SBOM tells you which libraries shipped, and says nothing about what trained the model beside them. Request a separate, explicit data provenance disclosure alongside any SBOM for an AI product, since the SBOM alone leaves the entire training data question genuinely unaddressed.

A useful and standard document to request from any AI vendor, but understand its real scope: it covers code components, not training data; do not treat receiving an SBOM as satisfying your data provenance due diligence, since they answer genuinely different questions.

A well-established artifact for conventional software component transparency that, when applied to AI products, leaves a genuine and significant gap around training data provenance; supply chain assessment for AI systems should require this document alongside, not instead of, separate data provenance evidence.

terms.origin: Standardized formats SPDX and CycloneDX; mandated in US federal procurement by EO 14028.
terms.example: Requiring an SBOM from an AI vendor while separately demanding training-data licensing terms.
terms.definition: An inventory of the components and dependencies inside a piece of software. It answers component provenance, not data licensing: an SBOM tells you which libraries shipped, and says nothing about what trained the model beside them.

lenses.body: A non-human account that a piece of software uses to log into and access another system. Unlike an AI agent, its behavior is completely predictable and always the same, which is exactly the trait that separates it from an agent that can decide what to do differently each time.

Its behavior is predictable, which is exactly what distinguishes it from an agent: a service principal does the same thing every night, an agent decides what to do next. Do not govern AI agent credentials using the same static permission model designed for predictable service principals, since an agent's variable, decision-driven behavior needs a genuinely different, more dynamic access control approach.

Understand that this well-established, predictable identity type is fundamentally different from an AI agent identity in a way that matters for governance; applying the same static access-control mental model to both can leave real gaps in oversight of the less predictable agent category.

A well-understood, predictable non-human identity category that should not be assumed to have the same risk profile or require the same governance approach as an AI agent identity, which exhibits meaningfully different, less predictable behavior warranting distinct oversight consideration.

terms.origin: Cloud identity-platform vocabulary, notably Microsoft Entra.
terms.example: Baselining a service principal's fixed access pattern so deviations alert immediately.
terms.definition: A non-human identity used by an application to authenticate to a service. Its behavior is predictable, which is exactly what distinguishes it from an agent: a service principal does the same thing every night, an agent decides what to do next.

lenses.body: The central system that collects security logs from all over a company and automatically flags suspicious patterns worth investigating. If AI usage logs never actually get sent into this system, then all that AI activity is essentially invisible to the security team, even though they are the ones responsible for watching for problems.

Its blind spot is whatever never reaches it, and AI gateway logs often never do, leaving the busiest new traffic channel invisible to the team paid to watch. Explicitly verify and configure AI gateway and inference endpoint logs to actually flow into your SIEM, since this integration is frequently missing by default and represents a real, currently common blind spot.

Ask your security team directly and specifically whether AI usage logs actually feed into your central security monitoring system; this is a common, easy-to-overlook gap, and an unmonitored high-volume traffic channel represents genuine, currently unaddressed risk.

A documented gap in security monitoring coverage specifically for AI-related traffic is a meaningful finding in any security assessment, since it represents a genuine and currently common blind spot in otherwise mature security operations programs that have not yet been extended to cover AI-specific traffic.

terms.origin: Established security operations category.
terms.example: Routing AI gateway and agent-action logs into the SIEM alongside firewall and endpoint feeds.
terms.definition: The platform that centralizes logs and correlates them into alerts. Its blind spot is whatever never reaches it, and AI gateway logs often never do, leaving the busiest new traffic channel invisible to the team paid to watch.

lenses.body: When a software company you already use quietly turns on a new AI feature inside their product, without you signing any new contract or agreeing to buy anything new. Because there was no purchase involved, it often never shows up in the usual list of "AI tools we use" that gets built by looking at contracts.

It is found in release notes, not purchase orders, which is why AI inventories built from contracts alone undercount what is actually running; build your AI inventory process to include vendor release-note monitoring for existing software, not only new procurement events, since this is a genuinely common and easily missed source of unaccounted AI exposure.

A real reason your organization's actual AI footprint is likely larger than any inventory built purely from procurement records; ask your team whether they actively monitor existing vendor release notes for newly enabled AI features, not just track new AI-specific purchases.

A common and underappreciated source of AI governance gaps, since organizations frequently have incomplete visibility into AI capability that arrived through an existing vendor relationship's feature update rather than a distinct, separately reviewed procurement event.

terms.example: A quarterly release-note review that catches a CRM enabling AI summarization by default.
terms.definition: A vendor switching on an AI feature inside software you already run, with no new contract and no procurement event. It is found in release notes, not purchase orders, which is why AI inventories built from contracts alone undercount what is actually running.

lenses.body: A report from an independent, outside auditor checking whether a company's security, uptime, and confidentiality controls actually work the way they claim. Companies buying software from other companies often specifically ask for this report before trusting a vendor with their data.

Always verify explicitly whether a vendor's AI-specific functionality falls within the actual audited scope of their SOC 2 report, since a report covering the vendor's core platform does not automatically extend to cover a newer, separately built or acquired AI feature unless the scope section specifically says so.

Its scope section is where AI services quietly fall inside or outside the attestation; read the actual scope section carefully rather than accepting the report's existence alone as sufficient assurance, since an AI feature added to a vendor's product after the audit scope was defined may not actually be covered by the attestation you are relying on.

A vendor's possession of a SOC 2 report is a meaningful but incomplete signal; the specific scope of what is actually covered, particularly for a newer AI feature layered onto an older audited platform, is where the real due diligence work is, worth verifying rather than assuming.

terms.origin: AICPA Trust Services Criteria.
terms.example: Reading a vendor's SOC 2 scope to confirm the AI feature actually sits within the audited boundary.
terms.definition: An attestation report on a service organization's controls over security, availability, and confidentiality, issued by an independent auditor. It is the report enterprise buyers ask for, and its scope section is where AI services quietly fall inside or outside the attestation.

lenses.body: A verified, trustworthy, signed record showing exactly where a piece of software, its containers, and its AI model weights actually came from, so a company can be sure they are running the genuine thing the vendor actually built, rather than something that got swapped or tampered with somewhere along the way.

It is what lets a deployer distinguish the artifact the vendor built from an artifact something substituted along the way; require signed provenance attestation for model weights and containers in your deployment pipeline, since this is what actually protects against a substituted or tampered artifact being deployed without detection.

A specific, verifiable technical control worth asking any critical AI vendor about; the absence of signed provenance for model weights and containers means your organization is trusting, without technical verification, that what is running is genuinely what the vendor intended to ship.

A verifiable, signed provenance chain for software and model artifacts is a meaningful supply-chain integrity control, and its absence represents a genuine, technically demonstrable gap in an organization's ability to detect a substituted or tampered artifact in its deployment pipeline.

terms.origin: Supply-chain security practice; frameworks include SLSA and Sigstore.
terms.example: Verifying a model file's signature against the publisher's key before loading it into production.
terms.definition: A verified record of where code, containers, and model weights originated, signed and traceable to a source. It is what lets a deployer distinguish the artifact the vendor built from an artifact something substituted along the way.

lenses.body: Carefully thinking through, before a system launches, all the different ways someone might try to attack it. For AI systems, this includes brand new kinds of questions that never used to matter: what can get delivered through the prompt box, what can sneak in through document lookups, and what can a tool the AI uses actually reach.

AI adds questions the old model never asked: what can the prompt channel deliver, what can retrieval import, what can a tool call reach. Explicitly extend your threat modeling template and process to include these AI-specific question categories, since a conventional web application threat model, however thorough, was not designed to prompt for these newer AI-specific attack vectors.

Confirm your security team's threat modeling process for AI systems specifically includes the newer categories of questions unique to AI, prompt channels, retrieval sources, tool access, rather than only reusing an existing conventional application threat modeling template that predates these considerations.

Documented threat modeling that explicitly addresses AI-specific attack vectors, prompt injection channels, retrieval poisoning, tool access abuse, is meaningfully stronger evidence of genuine risk assessment than a conventional threat model that predates and does not address these AI-specific considerations.

terms.origin: Established security-engineering practice; methods include STRIDE, from Microsoft.
terms.example: A design review that models prompt injection and retrieval poisoning alongside classic network threats.
terms.definition: Structured analysis of how a system could be attacked, done before it ships. AI adds questions the old model never asked: what can the prompt channel deliver, what can retrieval import, what can a tool call reach.

lenses.body: A well-known organizational structure that clearly separates three different jobs: the people who actually do the risky work and own that risk, a separate group that sets rules and watches over them, and a fully independent group that checks whether both of the first two groups are actually doing their jobs properly.

Position your AI governance and security function explicitly as second line, setting policy and monitoring, while ensuring the teams actually deploying and operating AI systems retain clear first-line risk ownership, and that internal audit maintains genuine third-line independence to check both.

AI governance sits in the second line: it sets policy and monitors, while the teams deploying AI own the risk and internal audit independently checks both. Make sure your organization's AI governance function is actually positioned as second line, distinct from both the teams deploying AI, first line, and internal audit, third line, since blurring these roles undermines the whole point of the structure.

A well-established, widely recognized organizational risk governance structure whose clear application to AI governance specifically, second line policy-setting and monitoring, distinct from first line risk ownership and third line independent assurance, is a meaningful indicator of organizational governance maturity.

terms.origin: Institute of Internal Auditors, Three Lines Model, 2020 revision.
terms.example: Assigning AI policy to risk, AI deployment risk to the business, and AI assurance to internal audit.
terms.definition: The IIA framework separating risk ownership (first line), oversight (second line), and independent assurance (third line). AI governance sits in the second line: it sets policy and monitors, while the teams deploying AI own the risk and internal audit independently checks both.

lenses.body: Limiting exactly which specific tools an AI agent is allowed to use, checked right at the moment it tries to use each one. The same agent doing two different jobs should actually get two different, narrower tool lists, each one containing only what that specific job genuinely needs, not one broad list covering everything it might ever do.

Scope it per workflow, not per agent: the same agent doing two jobs should hold two different tool sets, each as small as the job allows. Implement allowlisting at the workflow or task level rather than granting one broad, static tool set to an agent identity regardless of which specific task it is currently performing.

Ask specifically whether your deployed agents' tool access is scoped per task or broadly granted once and left static; the tighter, per-workflow scoping approach genuinely reduces blast radius if an agent is compromised or manipulated, at the cost of somewhat more configuration overhead.

Fine-grained, per-workflow tool allowlisting, rather than broad, static agent permissions, is a meaningful and demonstrable control reducing potential harm from a compromised or manipulated agent, worth specific attention in assessing an organization's agent governance maturity.

terms.example: A reporting workflow granting read-only tools while the same agent's filing workflow adds one write tool.
terms.definition: Restricting an agent to a defined set of tools evaluated at execution time. Scope it per workflow, not per agent: the same agent doing two jobs should hold two different tool sets, each as small as the job allows.

lenses.body: When an AI system uses way more computing resources than expected, costing a lot of money and using up capacity, whether that happens because of an attack, a bug, or an AI agent stuck in an accidental loop. Often the very first sign anyone notices is a shockingly large bill, not any kind of alert or warning beforehand.

It is OWASP LLM10, and in practice it is seen first on an invoice rather than in a dashboard; implement real-time usage monitoring with automatic circuit breakers, not just after-the-fact billing alerts, since waiting to discover this problem on an invoice means the damage, financial and potentially operational, has already fully occurred.

A real financial risk worth a specific question to your team: do we have real-time monitoring and automatic limits on AI usage, or would we only find out about a runaway cost event when the bill arrives? The second scenario is more common than it should be and entirely preventable.

A company without demonstrated real-time usage monitoring and automatic spending limits on their AI infrastructure carries genuine, underappreciated financial risk; ask specifically about this control, since a runaway consumption event can materially affect a quarter's costs with no advance warning.

terms.origin: OWASP LLM Top 10, category LLM10.
terms.example: A spend alert catching an integration retrying a failing model call thousands of times overnight.
terms.definition: Runaway inference volume that imposes cost and exhausts capacity, whether from attack, defect, or an agent loop. It is OWASP LLM10, and in practice it is seen first on an invoice rather than in a dashboard.

lenses.body: A digital identity given specifically to a running piece of software rather than to a person or a permanent application registration, commonly used in cloud computing. Its access only lasts exactly as long as that specific piece of software is actually running, which fits well with AI agent processes that start up and disappear quickly.

It narrows credentials to the workload's lifetime, which is the right shape for agent processes that spin up and vanish; prefer workload identity over longer-lived static credentials for ephemeral agent processes specifically, since the automatically time-bound nature of this credential type genuinely reduces the risk window compared to a static, long-lived credential.

A more secure default for short-lived, dynamically spun-up AI agent processes than a traditional, longer-lived credential; ask whether your organization's agent infrastructure uses this pattern, since it is a genuine, meaningful security improvement over static credentials for this specific, increasingly common use case.

A technically stronger identity pattern for ephemeral compute workloads, including AI agents, compared to static long-lived credentials, since its automatically time-bound nature inherently limits the exposure window in a way that requires no additional manual process to achieve.

terms.origin: Cloud-native identity practice; implementations include SPIFFE and cloud provider workload identity federation.
terms.example: A containerized agent authenticating through its workload identity instead of a shared API key.
terms.definition: An identity assigned to a running workload rather than to a person or an application registration, common in cloud and container platforms. It narrows credentials to the workload's lifetime, which is the right shape for agent processes that spin up and vanish.

lenses.body: Instead of trusting anyone already inside the building, you check everyone at every door, every time, even if they came in this morning.

No implicit trust from network position: every request is authenticated, authorised and evaluated against policy at access time. Applied to AI systems it means the model, the agent and the tool each hold their own identity, and a compromised component gains only what its own scope allows. NIST SP 800-207 is the reference architecture.

Practically, stop relying on being inside the perimeter. Every service call carries a verifiable identity, permissions are scoped narrowly and expire, and access decisions are made per request rather than at login. For AI features that means the agent gets its own credential with its own allowlist, never the calling user's full rights.

An architectural posture that produces per-request authorisation records, which is what makes access decisions auditable after the fact. It bears on security and accountability requirements, because it turns "who could have done this" from an inference about network topology into a logged decision.

terms.origin: Term popularized by Forrester, 2010; codified in NIST SP 800-207, 2020.
terms.example: Applying per-request verification to agent tool calls with the same rigor as user requests.
terms.definition: A security model that verifies every request rather than trusting network location. NIST SP 800-207 defines it, and it is rarely extended to agents: the architecture that never trusts a laptop still routinely trusts whatever an agent asks for once it is inside.

lenses.body: A little math switch inside an AI's brain-cells that lets it learn bendy, complicated patterns instead of only straight-line ones, kind of like a light dimmer instead of a simple on-off switch.

Choice of activation function (ReLU, GELU, SiLU) affects training stability and gradient flow more than most people expect; a hard-to-debug training instability is worth checking against activation choice before assuming it is a data or learning-rate problem.

Different activation functions produce measurably different loss landscapes and gradient behavior at scale, which is part of why activation choice remains an active architecture decision rather than a settled default, even in otherwise standardized transformer stacks.

Without nonlinearity, stacking layers adds nothing a single layer could not already do, since a chain of purely linear operations collapses mathematically into one linear operation, no matter how many layers you stack.

terms.example: ReLU, GELU, and SwiGLU are the common choices in modern models.
terms.definition: A nonlinear function applied to neuron outputs so the network can represent relationships more complex than straight lines. Without nonlinearity, stacking layers adds nothing a single layer could not do.

lenses.body: Imagine reading a long sentence and trying to work out who "she" refers to. Your eyes flick back to the name earlier in the sentence. Attention is the model doing that flicking back: for every word, it looks at all the other words and decides which ones matter for understanding this one.

Three projections per token (Q, K, V), a scaled dot product between Q and all K, a softmax, then a weighted sum of V. The practical consequence is memory, not maths: during generation you cache K and V for every past token, and that cache grows with context length and batch size until it, not compute, is what limits how many requests a GPU can serve.

The 2017 formulation removed recurrence and made sequence modelling parallel across positions, which is the property that made scaling practical. Most subsequent work is about the quadratic cost and the KV footprint: multi-query and grouped-query attention cut the number of key and value heads, and FlashAttention reorders the computation to be IO-aware without changing the output.

Attention lets a model weigh every token in the input against every other token, rather than reading strictly left to right. Each token produces a query, a key and a value; the query is compared against all keys to produce scores, and those scores blend the values. Because every pair is compared, cost grows with the square of sequence length.

terms.origin: Introduced in Bahdanau et al., 2014; made central by the 2017 transformer paper.
terms.example: A translation model attending to the right source word regardless of word order.
terms.definition: The component that weights the relevance of each input element when producing each output element, letting a model focus on what matters wherever it sits in the sequence. It is the core of the transformer and the reason context length costs compute.

lenses.body: An AI that squeezes information down small and then tries to rebuild it back to how it started. Whatever survives the squeezing is the important stuff; whatever gets lost was not that important.

Useful for anomaly detection and dimensionality reduction beyond generative pipelines; a data point the autoencoder reconstructs poorly is, by construction, one that does not fit the patterns it learned, which is a cheap and effective anomaly signal.

The bottleneck dimensionality is the key hyperparameter shaping what gets preserved versus discarded; too wide and the model can trivially copy input to output without learning useful structure, too narrow and genuinely relevant information gets lost.

What survives the squeeze is, by construction, the structure the data actually contains; the compression bottleneck forces the network to discard noise and redundancy while keeping whatever information is genuinely needed to reconstruct the input.

terms.example: Dimensionality reduction and image denoising pipelines.
terms.definition: A neural network that learns efficient encodings of unlabeled data by compressing it through an encoder and reconstructing it through a decoder. What survives the squeeze is, by construction, the structure the data actually contains.

lenses.body: An AI that writes its answer one word at a time, always looking back at everything it already wrote so far to decide the next word, like telling a story where each sentence depends on the one before it.

This is the reason retry-with-different-sampling strategies work as an error-recovery technique; since generation is sequential and conditioned on prior tokens, a fresh sample from the start can avoid a compounding error that a mid-generation correction cannot easily fix.

The sequential conditioning structure is exactly what non-autoregressive and diffusion-based text generation approaches attempt to escape, trading the compounding-error risk for a different and still-imperfect set of tradeoffs around global coherence and controllability.

Token-by-token generation is why LLM output streams visibly as it is produced, and it is also why an early wrong turn in the generation can compound through the rest of an answer, since each new token is conditioned on everything generated before it, including any mistake.

terms.example: A chat model producing a sentence one token at a time, each chosen in light of the last.
terms.definition: A model that generates each output conditioned on everything it has generated so far. Token-by-token generation is why LLM output streams, and why an early wrong turn can compound through the rest of an answer.

lenses.body: An AI trained so that a picture of a dog and the word "dog" end up sitting close together in its internal understanding, even though one is an image and one is text, which lets it match pictures to descriptions.

Widely used as a component rather than an end product; CLIP embeddings power image search, content moderation, and the text-conditioning step in many image generation pipelines, so understanding its embedding space is useful even if you never train a CLIP model yourself.

The contrastive training objective, pulling matched image-text pairs together and pushing mismatched pairs apart, is the key mechanism, and its known weaknesses, typographic attacks and certain compositional reasoning failures, remain active areas of follow-up work.

That shared alignment between images and text is specifically what makes zero-shot image classification and text-to-image retrieval work: the model can match a novel image to a text label it was never explicitly trained on that exact pairing for, because both landed in the same meaning space during training.

terms.origin: OpenAI, 2021, "Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision."
terms.example: Finding product photos from a text query with no task-specific training.
terms.definition: A model trained to align image and text embeddings in one shared space, so pictures and descriptions of the same thing land near each other. That alignment is what makes zero-shot image classification and text-to-image retrieval work.

lenses.body: An AI design built for pictures, that slides small pattern-detecting filters across an image to find edges, shapes, and textures, then combines those into an understanding of what the whole picture shows.

Still often the better choice for smaller datasets or edge deployment compared to vision transformers, since CNNs have useful built-in assumptions about images, like locality, that vision transformers must learn from data instead, requiring more training data to match CNN performance.

The inductive biases baked into the convolutional structure, translation invariance, locality, are precisely what vision transformers give up in exchange for flexibility, which is why ViT performance advantages only emerge reliably at larger data scales.

Dominated computer vision for roughly a decade and still runs much of production imaging today, even as transformer-based vision models have gained ground; CNNs remain the pragmatic choice for many resource-constrained or well-understood vision tasks.

terms.origin: LeCun et al., 1989; popularized at scale by AlexNet, 2012.
terms.example: Image classification and defect detection on a production line.
terms.definition: A deep learning architecture that processes visual data by sliding learned filters across an image, detecting edges, textures, and shapes at increasing levels of abstraction. It dominated computer vision for a decade and still runs much of production imaging.

lenses.body: A way for one AI part to look at and use information from a totally different part, like a translator reading the original sentence while writing the translation, instead of only looking at its own previous work.

This is the mechanism to inspect when a text-to-image model ignores part of your prompt; cross-attention maps can be visualized to see which prompt tokens actually influenced which regions of the generated image, which is a genuinely useful debugging tool.

Cross-attention weight visualization has become a standard interpretability tool for diagnosing prompt-following failures in conditional generation models, though the relationship between attention weight and actual causal influence remains a live methodological question.

It is how a decoder reads an encoder, and how an image generator reads a text prompt; the key structural difference from self-attention is that queries come from one sequence while keys and values come from a different sequence entirely, letting one stream consult another.

terms.example: A text prompt steering an image diffusion model through cross-attention layers.
terms.definition: Attention where the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another, letting one stream consult a second. It is how a decoder reads an encoder, and how an image generator reads a text prompt.

lenses.body: The part of an AI that writes the answer out one piece at a time, using both what it was given and everything it has already written so far, to figure out what comes next.

Decoder-only architectures dominate current general-purpose LLM deployment specifically because a single unified stack simplifies both training and serving infrastructure compared to maintaining separate encoder and decoder components.

The shift from encoder-decoder to decoder-only as the dominant paradigm for general language modeling is itself a notable architectural trend, driven largely by scaling behavior and training simplicity rather than a fundamental capability advantage for every task type.

GPT-style chat models are decoder-only: the same stack of layers both reads the prompt and writes the answer, which is architecturally simpler than an encoder-decoder split and turned out to scale very well for general-purpose language tasks.

terms.example: A decoder-only model completing text without a separate encoder stage.
terms.definition: The component that generates output tokens one at a time from a representation and the tokens produced so far. GPT-style chat models are decoder-only: the same stack reads the prompt and writes the answer.

lenses.body: An AI where every single part of its "brain" gets used for every single word it processes, as opposed to only using the relevant specialist parts, the way a full committee reviews every decision instead of just the right expert.

Easier to reason about and debug than a sparse mixture-of-experts model, with more predictable latency and no routing-related load-balancing concerns; a reasonable default choice unless you specifically need the capacity-per-compute advantage sparse architectures offer.

The scaling behavior of dense versus sparse models under fixed compute budgets remains an active comparison point in the literature, with sparse architectures generally winning on capacity-per-FLOP at the cost of added routing complexity and training instability risk.

Simpler to train and serve than sparse alternatives, at the price of spending full compute on every token whether that token actually needs the full model's capacity or not; the simplicity-versus-efficiency tradeoff is the core design choice against mixture-of-experts approaches.

terms.example: Classic transformer LLMs where each forward pass uses the whole network.
terms.definition: A model that activates all of its parameters for every token processed. Simpler to train and serve than sparse alternatives, at the price of spending full compute on every token whether the token needs it or not.

lenses.body: An AI that makes pictures or sounds by starting with random fuzzy noise and slowly cleaning it up, step by step, until a clear image or sound appears, like carefully wiping fog off a window bit by bit.

The number of denoising steps is a direct, tunable tradeoff between generation quality and speed; production applications typically use distilled or accelerated samplers to reduce steps needed, since the naive many-step process is too slow for interactive use.

The theoretical connection between diffusion models and score-based generative modeling, learning the gradient of the data distribution, unified what were initially separate research threads and continues to inform new sampler and training-objective designs.

Quality comes from many small denoising steps rather than one leap; this iterative refinement approach is what let diffusion models overtake GANs as the dominant image-generation paradigm, trading generation speed for more stable training and higher output diversity.

terms.origin: Ho et al., 2020, "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models."
terms.example: Stable Diffusion and Midjourney generating images from text prompts.
terms.definition: A class of generative models that create data by learning to reverse a noising process, iteratively removing noise until an image, video, or audio sample emerges. Quality comes from many small denoising steps rather than one leap.

lenses.body: A newer version of image-making AI that swaps out an older design for the same transformer building block used in chatbots, which turned out to work even better for pictures and videos as things get bigger.

If building or fine-tuning a media generation pipeline, DiT-based models generally offer better scaling headroom than U-Net-based predecessors, though tooling and community resources for U-Net architectures remain more mature as of this writing.

The transition from U-Net to transformer backbones in diffusion models mirrors the broader field pattern of transformer architectures displacing domain-specific designs once sufficient scale and data are available, consistent with the bitter lesson.

Most modern large media generators build on this design specifically because it brings the well-understood, favorable scaling behavior researchers already observed in transformer language models to image and video generation, replacing the older U-Net backbone.

terms.origin: Peebles and Xie, 2023, "Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers."
terms.example: Video generation models scaling quality by scaling the transformer backbone.
terms.definition: A diffusion model that replaces the U-Net backbone with a transformer, bringing transformer scaling behavior to image and video generation. Most modern large media generators build on this design.

lenses.body: The part of an AI that reads and understands the input and turns it into an internal summary the rest of the system can use, without necessarily writing anything new itself.

For pure classification or embedding tasks, an encoder-only model is usually cheaper and faster than using a full generative LLM; do not reach for a decoder-based chat model when an encoder-only model does the actual job better and at lower cost.

BERT-style encoder-only pretraining objectives, like masked language modeling, remain competitive for representation-learning tasks even as decoder-only autoregressive models have come to dominate general-purpose generation, reflecting a genuine task-dependent architecture tradeoff rather than a strict hierarchy.

Encoder-only models excel specifically at understanding tasks, classification, retrieval, similarity, where nothing needs to be generated as output; this is a genuinely different job than decoder-based generation and often a simpler, cheaper one for tasks that only require comprehension.

terms.example: BERT-style models embedding sentences for search.
terms.definition: The component that converts input into a dense representation the rest of the system can use. Encoder-only models excel at understanding tasks, classification, retrieval, and similarity, where nothing needs to be generated.

lenses.body: A two-part AI design: one part reads and understands the input, and a separate part writes the output, working together to turn one kind of thing, like a sentence in one language, into another, like the same sentence in a different language.

Still a reasonable architecture choice for well-defined sequence-to-sequence tasks with a fixed input and output structure, like machine translation, where the explicit separation can offer training efficiency advantages over a general decoder-only approach.

The relative advantages of encoder-decoder versus decoder-only architectures for sequence transformation tasks remain an area of ongoing comparison, with encoder-decoder models sometimes showing better sample efficiency on tasks with clear input-output structure despite decoder-only models' broader current adoption.

Translation and summarization were its home ground before decoder-only models absorbed most of those tasks; the natural fit is for tasks that clearly transform one full sequence into a different full sequence, though decoder-only architectures have proven flexible enough to handle these tasks too.

terms.example: T5 translating or summarizing by encoding the source and decoding the target.
terms.definition: An architecture pairing an encoder for the input with a decoder for the output, the natural shape for tasks that transform one sequence into another. Translation and summarization were its home ground before decoder-only models absorbed most tasks.

lenses.body: The part inside each layer of a transformer that processes each word by itself, separately from the attention part that compares words to each other. A lot of what the AI actually "knows" as facts is stored in these parts.

This is where mixture-of-experts routing typically replaces the standard dense FFN, since the FFN is usually the largest parameter count in a transformer block, making it the natural target for sparse capacity scaling.

Mechanistic interpretability work has increasingly localized specific factual associations and learned "circuits" to particular FFN neurons or activation patterns, which is part of why FFN layers are a current focus for knowledge editing and model interpretability research.

Much of what a model knows, its stored factual associations, lives specifically in these layers rather than in the attention mechanism; this is a notable and somewhat counterintuitive finding, since attention gets most of the public attention despite FFN layers holding much of the factual knowledge.

terms.example: Interpretability work locating factual recall in FFN weights.
terms.definition: The position-wise dense layers inside each transformer block, applied to every token independently between attention steps. Much of what a model knows, its stored factual associations, lives in these layers.

lenses.body: A clever way of doing the same attention math an AI already does, but organized so the computer's memory does much less work moving data around, which makes everything run a lot faster without changing the actual answer.

A near-free performance win worth enabling by default in any modern transformer training or inference stack; it produces mathematically identical results to standard attention while substantially reducing memory bandwidth requirements and often runtime as well.

A strong example of how hardware-aware algorithm design, rather than a new mathematical formulation, can unlock capability improvements; this pattern, optimizing for memory hierarchy rather than raw FLOP count, has informed subsequent kernel-level optimization work across the field.

Same mathematics, dramatically better hardware behavior, which is what made today's long context windows affordable; the innovation is entirely in how the computation is organized on the GPU, restructuring memory reads and writes, not in changing what attention actually computes.

terms.origin: Dao et al., 2022, "FlashAttention."
terms.example: Serving a long-context model at a fraction of the memory cost of naive attention.
terms.definition: A memory-efficient attention implementation that restructures the computation to minimize reads and writes to GPU memory. Same mathematics, dramatically better hardware behavior, which is what made today's long context windows affordable.

lenses.body: Two AIs competing against each other: one tries to make fake pictures good enough to fool the other, and the other tries to catch the fakes. As they compete, both get better, and the fake pictures get more and more realistic.

Mostly superseded by diffusion models for new image-generation projects due to training stability advantages, though GANs retain a speed advantage for real-time or latency-sensitive generation, since they produce output in a single forward pass rather than many denoising steps.

The training instability problems inherent to the minimax adversarial objective, mode collapse, vanishing gradients for the generator, motivated much of the theoretical work on alternative generative modeling objectives that eventually led to diffusion-based approaches.

The adversarial game produced the first convincingly realistic synthetic faces, but GANs are notoriously difficult to train stably, mode collapse and training instability are common failure modes, which is a significant part of why diffusion models have largely displaced them for high-quality image generation.

terms.origin: Goodfellow et al., 2014.
terms.example: Style transfer, super-resolution, and early deepfake generation.
terms.definition: An architecture in which two networks compete: a generator creates synthetic data and a discriminator judges real from fake, each improving against the other. The adversarial game produced the first convincingly realistic synthetic faces.

lenses.body: Making sure an AI's answers actually come from a real, checkable source instead of just what it remembers, so a grounded answer can point to where it got the information, and an ungrounded one is just asserting something without proof.

Design systems so grounded and ungrounded responses are visibly distinguishable to the user, ideally with an actual citation link; silently blending grounded retrieval with the model's own unsourced knowledge produces answers that look equally confident but carry very different reliability.

Faithfulness evaluation, measuring whether a grounded response actually reflects the cited source rather than merely being accompanied by one, remains a harder and less solved problem than retrieval itself, since a model can cite a real source while still misrepresenting its content.

A grounded answer can cite where it came from; an ungrounded one can only assert. This distinction is central to why retrieval-augmented generation matters: it converts an unverifiable claim from the model's parametric memory into a verifiable one anchored to a specific, checkable source document.

terms.example: A RAG system answering from retrieved policy documents and citing them.
terms.definition: Anchoring a model's responses to trusted sources rather than its parametric memory. A grounded answer can cite where it came from; an ungrounded one can only assert.

lenses.body: A way of storing facts as a web of connected dots and lines, like "Paris" connects to "France" which connects to "Europe," instead of just as separate sentences, which makes it easier to trace connections between related facts.

Worth pairing with vector-based retrieval rather than choosing one exclusively; knowledge graphs handle precise multi-hop relational queries well, while embedding-based retrieval handles fuzzy semantic similarity well, and the two approaches complement each other's weaknesses in a hybrid retrieval system.

Graph-augmented retrieval and graph-based reasoning over LLM outputs remain an active research area specifically because standard transformer attention has known limitations on genuinely multi-hop, structured reasoning tasks that graph traversal handles more naturally.

Paired with LLMs it supplies the precise, multi-hop structure that flat text retrieval loses; answering a question that requires chaining several facts together, like "who directed the movie that won the award the previous winner also won," is exactly what graph structure handles well and plain text search does not.

terms.example: An enterprise graph linking customers, contracts, and obligations for exact traversal.
terms.definition: A connected representation of entities and their relationships, storing facts as a network rather than rows. Paired with LLMs it supplies the precise, multi-hop structure that flat text retrieval loses.

lenses.body: A giant AI that has read an enormous amount of text and learned to understand, summarize, and write language really well, because it has absorbed a huge chunk of everything humans have ever written down.

Not every task needs a frontier-scale LLM; matching model size to task complexity, sometimes a small language model or a fine-tuned smaller model, meaningfully reduces cost and latency without a corresponding capability loss for well-bounded tasks.

The relationship between model scale and specific emergent capabilities remains only partially understood; scaling laws predict smooth improvement on aggregate metrics while individual capabilities can appear more discontinuously, which is an active area of interpretability and evaluation research.

Scale is the operative word: specific capabilities appear reliably only at sizes where the model has absorbed a meaningful fraction of written human knowledge, which is part of why smaller language models, while useful for bounded tasks, cannot simply be scaled down versions of the same broad capability.

terms.example: GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Claude handling drafting, analysis, and coding tasks.
terms.definition: A generative model trained on vast text corpora, capable of understanding, summarizing, generating, and predicting language. Scale is the operative word: capabilities appear at sizes where the model has absorbed a meaningful fraction of written human knowledge.

lenses.body: The AI's internal "map" of ideas, where similar concepts end up sitting close together, even ones from totally different examples, kind of like organizing a messy room so that similar things end up near each other.

Useful for building features like semantic search, similarity matching, and controlled generation via latent-space manipulation; understanding roughly how your model organizes its latent space helps explain otherwise puzzling output behavior.

Latent space geometry, including linear representation hypotheses and the discovery of interpretable directions corresponding to specific concepts, is a major current thread in mechanistic interpretability research, since navigable structure in this space suggests genuinely learned, organized representations rather than pure memorization.

Movement through this space is meaningful: interpolating between two points in latent space produces coherent blends of the concepts those points represent, which is the mechanism behind style-mixing in image generation and analogical reasoning behaviors observed in language models.

terms.example: Morphing between two faces by walking the latent space between them.
terms.definition: The compressed internal representation space where a model organizes what it has learned, with similar concepts sitting close together. Movement through this space is meaningful: interpolating between two points produces coherent blends.

lenses.body: A technique that keeps the numbers flowing through an AI's layers from getting too big or too small as they pass through, kind of like adjusting the volume at each step of a long chain of speakers so nobody has to shout or whisper.

Placement, pre-norm versus post-norm, is a real architectural choice with training-stability consequences, not a minor implementation detail; if you are debugging unstable training in a custom transformer, normalization placement is worth checking early.

The pre-norm versus post-norm debate connects directly to gradient flow theory in very deep networks; pre-norm's more stable gradients come with a tradeoff in final model performance under some conditions, which keeps this a live design consideration rather than a fully settled question.

Deep networks drift without it; pre-norm placement, applying normalization before rather than after each sublayer, is one specific reason very deep transformers train reliably, since it keeps gradient magnitudes more stable across many stacked layers than post-norm placement does.

terms.origin: Ba et al., 2016.
terms.example: Pre-norm transformer blocks in most modern LLMs.
terms.definition: A technique that normalizes activations within a layer to stabilize and speed training. Deep networks drift without it; pre-norm placement is one reason very deep transformers train reliably.

lenses.body: The raw, before-cleanup numbers an AI produces showing how much it favors each possible next word, before those numbers get turned into neat percentages that add up to 100%.

Inspect logits directly, not just the final sampled token, when debugging unexpected model output; the raw score distribution often reveals whether the model was genuinely confident, torn between close options, or essentially guessing, which the final chosen token alone does not show.

Logit lens and related interpretability techniques project intermediate-layer activations through the final unembedding to read out logits at earlier points in the network, offering a window into how the model's "answer" evolves layer by layer, which is a genuinely useful mechanistic interpretability tool.

They are the model's opinion in its most honest form, inspected for confidence and manipulated for steering; because logits are raw scores rather than normalized probabilities, they preserve more information about relative confidence and are the point where techniques like temperature scaling actually operate.

terms.example: Reading logits to measure how certain a classifier really was.
terms.definition: The raw, unnormalized scores a model produces before they are converted to probabilities. They are the model's opinion in its most honest form, inspected for confidence and manipulated for steering.

lenses.body: An older type of AI design that was good at remembering important information across long stretches of text or speech, using special internal "gates" that decide what to keep and what to forget.

Rarely the right default choice for a new project today given transformer alternatives, but still occasionally useful for resource-constrained, genuinely sequential streaming applications where transformer attention's memory requirements are prohibitive.

The inherently sequential, non-parallelizable nature of LSTM training, each timestep depends on the previous one's hidden state, is precisely the bottleneck that motivated the transformer's fully parallelizable attention mechanism, making LSTM limitations directly causal in the field's architectural shift.

Carried speech recognition and translation until transformers displaced it; the gating mechanism specifically solved the vanishing-gradient problem that crippled plain RNNs on long sequences, which was a genuine breakthrough at the time even though transformers have since become the dominant sequence architecture.

terms.origin: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997.
terms.example: Speech recognition and text generation systems of the pre-transformer era.
terms.definition: A recurrent architecture with gating that lets it retain information across long sequences, solving the vanishing-gradient problem that crippled plain RNNs. It carried speech recognition and translation until transformers displaced it.

lenses.body: A newer kind of AI design that can handle really long pieces of text efficiently, getting slower only in a straightforward, predictable way as text gets longer, instead of getting dramatically slower the way older attention-based designs do.

Worth evaluating specifically for very-long-context use cases where standard attention's quadratic memory cost becomes the bottleneck; tooling and pretrained model availability are less mature than for standard transformers, which is a real practical consideration.

Selective state space models represent a genuine architectural alternative to attention rather than an incremental optimization, and the empirical comparison of pure SSM, pure attention, and hybrid architectures across task types remains an active and unsettled area of research.

Hybrid designs pair Mamba layers with transformer layers specifically to get length efficiency without giving up attention's strengths; attention's quadratic cost with sequence length becomes prohibitive for very long inputs, which is the specific problem this linear-time alternative addresses.

terms.origin: Gu and Dao, 2023.
terms.example: Hybrid Mamba-transformer models serving very long documents cheaply.
terms.definition: A selective state space model offering long-context processing with linear time complexity, against attention's quadratic cost. Hybrid designs pair Mamba layers with transformer layers to get length efficiency without giving up attention's strengths.

lenses.body: A shared, standard way for AI models to connect to tools and information, so a tool only has to be built to work with this one standard, instead of being rebuilt separately for every different AI company's system.

Adopting this standard for a new tool integration is usually the right default over a custom, model-specific integration, since it means the integration works with any MCP-compliant model rather than being locked to one provider's specific API.

As an emerging standard, MCP's security model, particularly around trust boundaries when an agent consumes content from an untrusted MCP server, is a genuinely open area worth close attention, since standardized tool access also standardizes the attack surface.

The plumbing standard of the agent era: an MCP server exposes a capability once, and any compliant model can use it, which is the same "build it once, use it everywhere" logic that made earlier technology standards, like USB or HTTP, valuable beyond any single implementation.

terms.origin: Anthropic, November 2024; subsequently adopted across the industry.
terms.example: A company exposing its CRM through one MCP server that every AI assistant can call.
terms.definition: An open standard for connecting AI models to tools and data sources through a common interface, so integrations are built once rather than per-model. It is the plumbing standard of the agent era: an MCP server exposes a capability, and any compliant model can use it.

lenses.body: An AI design with many specialist "expert" sections inside it, where a router decides which few experts should handle each specific word, so the AI has a lot of total knowledge but does not have to use all of it every single time.

Serving infrastructure for MoE models is meaningfully more complex than for dense models, since routing decisions and expert load balancing add operational considerations that a simple dense-model deployment does not have; budget for that complexity if adopting this architecture.

Router training instability and expert load imbalance remain persistent open engineering problems in MoE architectures; auxiliary load-balancing losses help but do not fully solve the tendency for routing to collapse onto a small subset of experts during training.

It buys large total capacity at modest per-token compute, since only a few experts fire per token; this means a mixture-of-experts model can have far more total parameters than a dense model while costing roughly the same to run per token, which is the core economic argument for the architecture.

terms.origin: Shazeer et al., 2017, "Outrageously Large Neural Networks."
terms.example: Mixtral routing each token through two of eight experts.
terms.definition: An architecture combining multiple specialized sub-networks with a router that decides which experts process each input. It buys large total capacity at modest per-token compute, since only a few experts fire per token.

lenses.body: Running several attention "checks" on the same sentence at the same time, each one looking for a different kind of pattern, like one checking grammar while another checks which words refer to the same thing, then combining all those checks together.

The number of attention heads is a tunable hyperparameter with real tradeoffs; more heads can capture more relationship types but increase compute cost, and the useful default range is well established in the literature for most model sizes rather than needing extensive tuning per project.

Attention head interpretability, identifying what specific relationship or pattern individual heads specialize in, is a well-developed subfield of mechanistic interpretability, though the degree to which heads are cleanly interpretable versus entangled remains model- and layer-dependent.

Standard in every transformer block: one head tracking syntax while another tracks reference is a common informal description, though the actual specialization any given head learns emerges from training rather than being explicitly assigned, and varies across models and layers.

terms.origin: Vaswani et al., 2017.
terms.example: Separate heads attending to a pronoun's antecedent and its verb at once.
terms.definition: Running several attention operations in parallel so the model captures different relationship types simultaneously, one head tracking syntax while another tracks reference. Standard in every transformer block.

lenses.body: AI that can work with more than one kind of information at once, like reading text, looking at pictures, and listening to sound, all inside the same system, instead of needing separate AI tools for each one.

Test each modality's handling independently as well as jointly; a multimodal model can be strong on text and weak on image reasoning, or vice versa, and aggregate benchmark scores can mask significant per-modality weakness that matters for your specific use case.

Cross-modal alignment quality, how well the model actually integrates information across modalities rather than processing each in isolation and superficially combining outputs, remains a genuine and only partially solved evaluation challenge distinct from per-modality capability.

The practical effect is that a single interface can read a chart, hear a meeting, and answer in prose within one continuous interaction, which is a meaningfully different user experience than chaining together separate single-purpose tools for each modality.

terms.example: GPT-4o and Gemini analyzing an uploaded diagram and discussing it in text.
terms.definition: Models that process, understand, and generate multiple data types, text, images, audio, video, within one system. The practical effect is that a single interface can read a chart, hear a meeting, and answer in prose. Sometimes shortened to simply multimodal.

lenses.body: A computer system loosely inspired by how brain cells connect to each other, built from many simple connected pieces whose connection strengths get adjusted based on examples during training, until it learns to do something useful.

Architecture choice, CNN, transformer, or other, matters far more than the underlying "neural network" label suggests; treat the specific architecture as the meaningful engineering decision, since "we use a neural network" alone conveys almost no useful information about the system's actual design.

The biological inspiration is now largely historical and loose rather than mechanistically precise; modern deep learning theory and practice have diverged substantially from neuroscience, and treating the "neural" framing as a literal brain analogy tends to mislead rather than inform current architecture research.

Every deep learning system, from image classifiers to large language models, is a neural network at heart; the enormous variety of specific architectures, CNNs, transformers, and others, are all different structural arrangements of this same fundamental building block, learned connection weights adjusted through training.

terms.origin: McCulloch and Pitts, 1943; modern form via backpropagation, 1986.
terms.example: Feedforward networks underlying all of deep learning.
terms.definition: A computing system inspired by biological neural networks, built from interconnected nodes whose connection strengths are learned from data. Every deep learning system, from image classifiers to LLMs, is a neural network at heart.

lenses.body: A trick for telling an AI where each word sits in a sentence, since otherwise the AI would just see a jumbled bag of words with no sense of order, unable to tell "dog bites man" apart from "man bites dog."

RoPE has become the de facto standard positional method in most modern open models over older fixed sinusoidal encodings, largely due to its better extrapolation behavior to sequence lengths beyond what the model was trained on.

Length extrapolation behavior, how well a model handles sequences longer than its training context, differs meaningfully across positional encoding schemes and remains an active area of comparison, since different methods make different implicit assumptions about how position information should generalize.

Without it, attention cannot distinguish "dog bites man" from "man bites dog," since the self-attention mechanism itself is fundamentally order-agnostic, treating input as an unordered set unless position information is explicitly injected some other way.

terms.origin: Vaswani et al., 2017.
terms.example: Sinusoidal or learned encodings added to token embeddings.
terms.definition: A method for injecting token-order information into a model that otherwise sees an unordered set. Without it, attention cannot distinguish "dog bites man" from "man bites dog."

lenses.body: An older AI design for handling sequences, like sentences or sound, where the network loops back on itself so that what it processed earlier can still influence what it does now, one step at a time in order.

Rarely the right choice for a new project today given transformer alternatives' parallel training advantage, though understanding the sequential-dependency limitation remains useful context for why current architectures are designed the way they are.

The sequential computation bottleneck in RNNs is the direct historical motivation for the transformer's design; understanding this causal lineage is useful context for evaluating newer linear-attention and state-space alternatives that in some ways revisit RNN-like recurrence with modern training-efficiency solutions.

It defined sequence modeling before attention, and its inability to parallelize training, since each timestep genuinely depends on completing the previous one, is what transformers specifically fixed, unlocking the massive parallel-hardware training that made today's model scale possible.

terms.example: Time-series forecasting and pre-transformer translation systems.
terms.definition: A network class for sequential data in which connections loop, letting past inputs influence present processing. It defined sequence modeling before attention, and its inability to parallelize training is what transformers fixed.

lenses.body: A shortcut wire in an AI that lets information skip past a layer and add directly to what comes out the other side, which helps very deep AIs, ones with hundreds of layers, actually learn properly instead of getting stuck.

A now-standard, essentially non-negotiable component of any deep transformer or CNN architecture; if implementing a custom deep network from scratch and it fails to train past a modest depth, missing or misplaced residual connections are a common and worth-checking first cause.

The residual stream framing, viewing the network as repeatedly reading from and writing to a persistent additive stream rather than a strict sequential pipeline, has become a central lens in mechanistic interpretability research for understanding how information flows and accumulates through transformer layers.

The structural trick that made networks hundreds of layers deep trainable at all; it gives gradients a direct path backward through the network during training, avoiding the vanishing-gradient problem that made very deep networks nearly impossible to train before this innovation.

terms.origin: He et al., 2015, "Deep Residual Learning."
terms.example: Standard in every deep architecture since ResNet.
terms.definition: A skip connection that adds a layer's input to its output, giving gradients a direct path through deep networks. It is the structural trick that made networks hundreds of layers deep trainable at all.

lenses.body: A clever mathematical trick for telling an AI how far apart two words are from each other in a sentence, done in a way that still works well even for much longer sentences than it originally trained on.

If extending a model's context length beyond its original training range, RoPE-based scaling techniques, like position interpolation or NTK-aware scaling, are the standard tools; know which positional scheme your base model uses before attempting any context extension.

RoPE's extrapolation behavior degrades in specific, characterized ways beyond certain length thresholds, which has motivated a family of follow-up scaling techniques; understanding these failure modes is prerequisite to evaluating claims about a model's effective long-context capability.

It extrapolates to longer sequences better than fixed encodings, which is specifically why most modern open models use it; encoding relative rather than absolute position directly into the attention computation gives the model a more generalizable sense of distance between tokens.

terms.origin: Su et al., 2021, "RoFormer."
terms.example: Llama-family models handling contexts longer than trained lengths.
terms.definition: A positional method that rotates query and key vectors by position-dependent angles, encoding relative position directly into attention. It extrapolates to longer sequences better than fixed encodings, which is why most modern open models use it.

lenses.body: The traffic-controller part of a mixture-of-experts AI that decides which specialist experts should handle each specific word, so the AI uses only the relevant specialists instead of running every specialist on every single word.

Monitor expert utilization in production if serving an MoE model; a router that has drifted toward heavily favoring a few experts indicates a load-balancing problem that is degrading the efficiency benefit the architecture was chosen for in the first place.

Router collapse and the auxiliary losses designed to prevent it remain an active area of MoE training research; the tension between letting the router specialize naturally and forcing balanced expert utilization through auxiliary objectives is not fully resolved.

Routing quality determines whether capacity is used or wasted, and load balancing across experts is its persistent engineering problem; a poorly trained router can collapse onto favoring a small subset of experts, effectively wasting the extra capacity the mixture-of-experts design was meant to provide.

terms.example: A router spreading tokens evenly so no expert sits idle while another saturates.
terms.definition: The component in a mixture-of-experts model that selects which experts process each token. Routing quality determines whether capacity is used or wasted, and load balancing across experts is its persistent engineering problem.

lenses.body: The part of a transformer that lets every word in a sentence look at and consider every other word, no matter how far apart they are, to figure out which ones matter most for understanding each other.

The quadratic compute and memory cost of self-attention with sequence length is the specific practical constraint driving both context-window pricing and the development of alternative architectures like state space models for very long inputs.

The full pairwise comparison structure of self-attention is both its core strength, direct long-range interaction, and its core cost, quadratic scaling, which continues to motivate a substantial body of research into sparse, linear, and approximate attention variants.

It is what gives transformers their grasp of long-range context; unlike older sequential architectures where information had to pass through many intermediate steps to connect distant words, self-attention lets any two tokens interact directly regardless of their distance in the sequence.

terms.origin: Vaswani et al., 2017, "Attention Is All You Need."
terms.example: Resolving what "it" refers to across a long paragraph.
terms.definition: The transformer component that lets every token weigh its relationship to every other token in the sequence, regardless of distance. It is what gives transformers their grasp of long-range context.

lenses.body: Searching by what something actually means instead of by matching exact words, so it can find the right answer to your question even if the answer uses completely different words than the ones you typed.

Combine semantic search with traditional keyword search in a hybrid approach for most production retrieval systems; semantic search excels at conceptual matches but can sometimes miss exact-term precision that keyword search handles more reliably, like exact product codes or names.

Embedding model choice significantly affects semantic search quality in domain-specific applications, and general-purpose embedding models often underperform domain-fine-tuned alternatives on specialized vocabulary, which remains a practical gap between benchmark performance and real deployment quality.

It finds the document that answers the question even when the question shares no words with it, which is the specific capability that keyword-based search lacks; the underlying mechanism compares numerical embeddings representing meaning rather than matching literal text strings.

terms.example: A query for "reducing churn" surfacing a document titled "customer retention playbook."
terms.definition: Retrieval based on meaning rather than keyword overlap, implemented by comparing embeddings. It finds the document that answers the question even when the question shares no words with it.

lenses.body: A smaller, lighter version of a big AI, built to run fast and fit on smaller devices like a phone, trading away some of the biggest model's abilities in exchange for speed and not needing an internet connection.

Evaluate task-specific performance on your actual use case before assuming a frontier model is necessary; a well-chosen or fine-tuned small model frequently matches large-model performance on narrow, bounded tasks at a fraction of the cost and latency.

Knowledge distillation from larger teacher models into smaller student models is a major technique for building capable SLMs, and the gap between distilled small-model performance and native large-model performance on specific benchmarks continues to narrow as distillation methods improve.

The trade is deliberate: for bounded tasks, a small model that runs locally beats a frontier model that requires a round trip, since the latency and cost of a network call to a large remote model can outweigh the capability advantage for a narrow, well-defined task.

terms.example: Phi and Gemma-class models running on a laptop for classification tasks.
terms.definition: A lightweight language model optimized for speed, memory footprint, and edge deployment rather than maximum capability. The trade is deliberate: for bounded tasks, a small model that runs locally beats a frontier model that requires a round trip.

lenses.body: The math step that turns a bunch of raw scores into neat percentages that all add up to 100%, so an AI can treat its options as proper probabilities instead of just arbitrary numbers.

Temperature scaling works by dividing logits before applying softmax; understanding this mechanism explains why higher temperature produces more varied output, it flattens the resulting probability distribution, making less-likely tokens more competitive for selection.

Softmax's exponential normalization has known numerical stability considerations at implementation level, and alternative normalization functions have been explored in specific architecture variants, though softmax remains the standard choice for the final output distribution in nearly all current models.
