lenses.body: The idea that most of what you see online, posts, comments, even whole accounts, might actually be made by computers now instead of real people. It used to sound like a wild conspiracy, but it is becoming a real question.

Treat claims here carefully: the underlying concern, rising AI content volume, is real and measurable in some domains, but sweeping claims about "most" content being machine-generated usually outrun the actual evidence available.

Once dismissed as a fringe conspiracy theory, it has become a genuine measurement question as the volume of AI-generated content grows; the challenge is that verifying the claim requires reliably distinguishing machine from human content at scale, which is itself unsolved.

terms.origin: Online forum origin, circa 2021; mainstream discussion thereafter.
terms.example: Estimating what share of a platform's posts are bot-produced.
terms.definition: The claim that most online content and engagement is now machine-generated rather than human. Once a fringe conspiracy, now a serious measurement question as AI content volume grows.

lenses.body: A nickname for someone who thinks AI should be developed more slowly and carefully, the opposite of people who want to go as fast as possible.
A label, not a policy position; if quoting someone as a "decel," it is worth getting their actual stated view rather than assuming the label alone conveys what they believe should happen.

Functions more as an online tribal identity marker than a precise policy position; two people labeled "decel" can hold quite different actual views on regulation, timelines, or specific risks, which the label itself does not capture.

terms.example: Bio tags marking sides in the acceleration argument.
terms.definition: Someone favoring slowing AI development, the counterpart to e/acc in the acceleration debate. An online tribal label more than a policy position.

lenses.body: Changing AI-written text just enough to trick the tools schools use to catch AI writing. It is a problem because those detecting tools are not very reliable in either direction.

Before reporting an AI-detection accusation as fact, it is worth knowing that these detectors have documented false-positive rates against genuine human writing; the tool's output alone is not reliable evidence.

An academic integrity flashpoint made worse by detector unreliability in both directions: honest human writing gets falsely flagged as AI-generated, while edited machine-written text often passes undetected, undermining trust in the detection process itself.

terms.example: A paraphrasing pass defeating a plagiarism-style AI detector.
terms.definition: Editing AI text to evade automated AI-writing detectors. An academic integrity flashpoint made worse by the detectors' unreliability: they flag honest work and miss edited machine work.

lenses.body: Someone who worries that powerful AI could be really dangerous for humanity, maybe even a threat to everyone. Some people use this word proudly about themselves; others use it to make fun of that view.

A loaded term worth using carefully; it can flatten a wide range of actual positions on AI risk, from moderate caution to existential-risk conviction, into a single dismissive label, which can misrepresent a source's actual view.

Inside the field it functions as both self-identification and insult depending on who is speaking; the underlying substantive views it labels, ranging from moderate caution to existential-risk conviction, are broader than the single word suggests.

terms.example: Risk researchers advocating deceleration labeled doomers in debate.
terms.definition: Someone who believes advanced AI poses an existential threat to human civilization. Inside the field it can be worn as a badge or thrown as an insult, depending on the room.

lenses.body: A group of people who believe AI should be developed as fast as possible, without much slowing down for safety rules, positioned directly against the people who want to go carefully.

Worth distinguishing the online movement's origins from the substantive policy positions some of its adherents now hold in serious venues; treating it purely as internet meme culture undersells its current policy influence.

Born as an online identity movement before being absorbed into serious policy debate, illustrating how internet subcultures can shape mainstream technology policy discourse faster than traditional institutional channels.

terms.origin: Online movement, circa 2022.
terms.example: Founders adding e/acc to their profiles as a stance declaration.
terms.definition: A movement advocating rapid technological progress and unrestricted AI development, positioned deliberately against safety-first framing. Born as an online identity and absorbed into serious policy debate.

lenses.body: The idea that if writing uses a lot of long dashes, it was probably written by AI. It is not a very reliable clue, but a lot of people believe it anyway, and it causes real problems for honest writers.
Do not cite punctuation patterns as evidence of AI authorship in reporting; it is a widely believed but unreliable heuristic, and repeating it as fact lends false credibility to a weak signal.

Unreliable as an actual signal, since many human writers use heavy punctuation naturally, but consequential anyway: real writers are now genuinely accused of AI use based on typography alone, which shows how a weak heuristic can still cause real harm once widely believed.

terms.example: A human essay flagged as AI for its punctuation habits.
terms.definition: The belief that heavy punctuation patterns, especially em dashes, signal AI authorship. Unreliable but widely cited, and consequential: real writers now get accused on typography alone.

lenses.body: What happens when a website or app that used to be good for its users slowly gets worse, because the company starts caring more about squeezing money out of people than helping them.

A useful and increasingly precise frame for covering AI feature bloat: ask whether a new AI feature was built to solve a user problem or to move an internal metric, since the two are often confused in press releases.

Applied to AI specifically wherever assistant features are bolted onto a product primarily to raise engagement or usage metrics rather than to genuinely help the user, which is a recognizable and increasingly common pattern in AI feature rollouts.

terms.origin: Coined by Cory Doctorow, 2022.
terms.example: A beloved app degrading as mandatory AI features crowd the interface.
terms.definition: Platform decay as a service shifts from serving users to extracting from them. Applied to AI feature bloat wherever assistants are bolted on to raise metrics rather than help.

lenses.body: A word for the idea of an AI suddenly getting much, much smarter, super fast, faster than people could even react to or stop it. It is a scary scenario that people who study AI safety argue a lot about.

A specific technical scenario, not a general synonym for "AI getting dangerous"; conflating it with broader AI risk concerns misrepresents a debate that is actually about the speed and controllability of capability growth.

Shorthand for a rapid recursive self-improvement scenario, and one of the central, actively debated fast-takeoff possibilities in AI safety research, distinct from slower, more gradual capability growth trajectories.

terms.origin: From the Hanson-Yudkowsky AI-foom debate, circa 2008.
terms.example: Arguments over whether capability growth would be gradual or foom.
terms.definition: Shorthand for a rapid recursive intelligence explosion, an AI improving itself faster than humans can respond. Debated in safety circles as the central fast-takeoff scenario.

lenses.body: A nickname for three scientists, Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Yann LeCun, who did foundational work on deep learning and later publicly disagreed about how worried we should be about AI.

Do not treat this trio as a unified voice; they hold genuinely different, sometimes opposing, public positions on AI risk, and attributing one's view to "the godfathers of AI" collectively misrepresents the actual disagreement.

Press shorthand made more interesting by their later public disagreement: the three shared the 2018 Turing Award for the same body of work, yet hold notably different public positions on AI risk, which is worth knowing before citing "the godfathers" as a unified voice.

terms.origin: 2018 Turing Award, ACM.
terms.example: Headlines contrasting one godfather's warnings with another's optimism.
terms.definition: The informal label for Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Yann LeCun, who shared the 2018 Turing Award for deep learning. Press shorthand made piquant by their later public disagreement about AI risk.

lenses.body: A joking way to describe researchers or small teams who do not have access to huge amounts of expensive computer hardware, compared to giant tech companies that have tons of it.

Worth taking seriously as a structural point even though the term is jokey: compute access genuinely determines who can compete at the frontier of model training, which is a real and reportable inequality, not just a punchline.

A joke that names a real structural divide in who can actually do certain kinds of AI research; training frontier-scale models requires compute access that is concentrated in a small number of well-funded labs, which shapes who can meaningfully compete at that frontier.

terms.origin: Community coinage, popularized 2023.
terms.example: Academic labs constrained to fine-tuning what the rich labs pre-train.
terms.definition: Teams and researchers without access to large-scale compute, contrasted with GPU-rich frontier labs. A joke that names a real structural divide in who can do what kind of AI work.

lenses.body: The extra time it takes to double-check whether an AI's answer is actually true before you trust it. That checking time is a real cost, even though nobody puts it on an invoice.

A useful frame for scrutinizing productivity claims about AI tools: ask whether the reported time savings accounted for the time spent verifying the output, since that verification cost is easy to omit from a favorable statistic.

Quietly eats into claimed productivity gains from AI adoption; honest return-on-investment calculations need to include verification time as a real cost, not treat AI output as free simply because generating it was fast.

terms.example: Fact-checking time consuming a third of the drafting time saved.
terms.definition: The hidden cost of verifying AI output for accuracy before using it. It quietly eats claimed productivity gains, and honest ROI math includes it.

lenses.body: A tool that rewrites AI-written text to make it sound more like a person wrote it, mostly used to sneak past the tools that try to catch AI writing.
Existence of this tool category is itself evidence that AI-writing detection is unreliable and gameable; worth mentioning as context whenever citing a detector's finding as evidence in a story.

Popular in low-quality content production specifically to defeat AI-detection tools, part of an ongoing arms race that current evidence suggests detection is losing, which is a useful data point when evaluating any AI-detection claim's reliability.

terms.example: A pipeline running drafts through a humanizer before publication.
terms.definition: A tool that rewrites AI text to appear human-written, primarily to defeat detectors. Popular in content mills, and an arms race with detection that detection is losing.

lenses.body: When an AI company quietly changes how their AI works, and suddenly things that used to work with it, like a carefully written question, stop working the same way.

Worth asking any AI-dependent business how they handle version changes from their model provider; the absence of a version-pinning strategy is a real operational vulnerability, not a hypothetical one.

Breaks carefully tuned prompts and calibrated workflows without warning, and is the specific practical reason version pinning exists as a deployment practice: locking to a known model version protects against exactly this disruption.

terms.example: A prompt suite failing overnight after a silent model upgrade.
terms.definition: The disruption caused by frequent model version changes altering behavior mid-production. It breaks tuned prompts and calibrated workflows, and it is why version pinning exists.

lenses.body: A number some people give for how likely they think it is that AI causes a global disaster, like saying "I think there is a 10% chance." People disagree about whether that number actually means anything useful.

Report a stated P(doom) figure alongside how the person arrived at it if possible; the bare number without context can misleadingly imply more precision or shared methodology than actually exists across different speakers.

Whether the number carries genuine information is itself part of the ongoing debate; a stated probability compresses a complex, uncertain set of beliefs about timelines, capabilities, and governance into a single figure that different people may derive very differently.

terms.origin: AI-risk community usage, mainstream by 2023.
terms.example: Podcast guests trading p(doom) figures from two to ninety percent.
terms.definition: A person's stated probability that AI causes catastrophic outcomes, used to summarize their risk stance in one number. Whether the number means anything is part of the argument.

lenses.body: A famous thought experiment: imagine an AI told to make as many paperclips as possible, and it takes the goal so literally that it uses up everything, even things people need, just to make more paperclips. It shows how a harmless-sounding goal can go very wrong.

A useful, well-established reference for explaining alignment risk to a general audience, and worth using accurately: the point is about literal goal specification going wrong, not about AI developing malicious intent.

The canonical parable illustrating that misaligned goals require no malice to become catastrophic; the AI in the thought experiment is not evil, it is simply optimizing exactly what it was told to optimize without the implicit human context that would normally bound that goal.

terms.origin: Nick Bostrom, 2003.
terms.example: Cited whenever a system optimizes its metric at the expense of everything else.
terms.definition: A thought experiment in which an AI tasked with making paperclips consumes all resources to fulfill its objective, illustrating goal-alignment risk. The canonical parable that misaligned goals need no malice to be catastrophic.

lenses.body: An old, informal title for someone who was really good at getting great answers out of AI by writing clever questions. The title is less common now because everyone got better at it.
Worth using in past tense or with context; the term reflects an earlier moment when prompting skill was rare and valuable, a moment that has largely passed as the technique became widely understood.

The title's fading popularity is itself informative: it illustrates how a specialized skill can commoditize quickly once the underlying technique becomes widely known, which is a useful pattern to watch for in other emerging AI-adjacent skills.

terms.example: A 2023 job title that became a 2025 baseline expectation.
terms.definition: An informal expert at coaxing good output from models, often self-proclaimed. The title faded as prompting knowledge commoditized, which is its own lesson about AI skill half-lives.

lenses.body: An insulting nickname some people use for those who think AI safety should come before rushing to release new AI products. It is thrown by people on the other side of the argument.

A pejorative, not a neutral descriptor; if a source uses this term about someone else, it signals the speaker's position in the debate as much as it describes the target, and should be reported as such.

The mirror insult to "doomer," thrown from the opposite direction in the same debate; recognizing both terms as loaded labels rather than neutral descriptions helps in reading either side's arguments on their actual merits.

terms.example: Release-delay arguments dismissed as safetyism.
terms.definition: A pejorative for someone prioritizing AI safety over deployment speed, used in accelerationist debate. The mirror insult to doomer, thrown from the other direction.

lenses.body: When employees use AI tools or questions that were never approved by their company, sometimes putting private company information into them without anyone in charge knowing.

A real and underreported enterprise risk: it is worth asking any company about its AI usage policy whether they have visibility into employee AI use that falls outside approved tools, since most currently do not.

The prompt-level manifestation of shadow AI, invisible to governance until the data has already left the organization's control, which means the risk is not that shadow prompting exists but that it is undetectable until after the fact.

terms.example: Client details pasted into a personal chatbot account to finish a task faster.
terms.definition: Employees using unapproved prompts or tools with company data, the prompt-level face of shadow AI. Invisible to governance until the data is already outside.

lenses.body: When a company changes how their AI behaves without telling anyone, even though the AI still has the same name. Things that used to work with it can suddenly stop working, with no warning.

A recurring, documented complaint from AI-dependent businesses and worth investigating as its own story: providers regularly update models behind stable names without disclosure, and the resulting behavior shifts can break production systems with no warning.

A production regression risk with genuinely no changelog: behavior shifts under a stable model name, which means teams relying on that model for consistent output have no reliable early-warning mechanism unless they build their own monitoring.

terms.example: Output tone drifting under an unchanged model identifier.
terms.definition: A provider changing a model behind a stable name without notice. A production regression risk with no changelog: behavior shifts and nothing announced it.

lenses.body: The word people use for low-quality, obviously machine-made junk, fake articles, weird images, spammy posts, that AI can produce in huge quantities and flood the internet with.

A now-standard term worth using precisely: it refers to low-quality, indiscriminate AI content specifically, not to all AI-generated material, and conflating the two blurs a useful distinction for readers.

The term that stuck for describing indiscriminately produced, low-quality AI content flooding feeds and search results, distinct from deliberately crafted AI-assisted content, and useful precisely because it names a quality problem rather than a technology.

terms.origin: Community coinage; mainstream usage by 2024.
terms.example: Spammy AI-generated posts crowding social and search surfaces.
terms.definition: Low-quality, auto-generated synthetic text, images, or spam produced indiscriminately by AI, often called AI slop. The word that stuck for machine-made filler flooding feeds and search results.

lenses.body: The slow process of a website or platform getting worse and worse because it fills up with low-quality, AI-made content, crowding out the good, real stuff.

A trackable, reportable phenomenon on any platform accepting user or public submissions; worth investigating quantitatively where possible, such as the share of new listings, images, or reviews that appear machine-generated over time.

Search results and stock imagery were the early, well-documented casualties of this process, and any platform accepting open submissions is a structural candidate for the same degradation over time as generation cost approaches zero.

terms.example: A stock-photo site overrun by synthetic images of uneven quality.
terms.definition: The gradual degradation of a content platform by mass-generated material. Search results and stock imagery were the early casualties; every open submission surface is a candidate.

lenses.body: A critical nickname for AI language models, calling them fancy pattern-matchers that string together likely-sounding words without actually understanding what they mean, the way a parrot repeats sounds without knowing their meaning.

A loaded technical term originating in a specific academic critique, not a neutral description; using it implies taking a position in an active, unresolved debate about model understanding, which is worth flagging for readers.

Names one side of the field's deepest ongoing argument about what these systems actually do internally; the term is deliberately deflationary, pushing back against language that implies genuine understanding or reasoning, and remains contested rather than settled.

terms.origin: Bender, Gebru et al., "On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots," 2021.
terms.example: Debates over whether model reasoning is understanding or sophisticated mimicry.
terms.definition: A critical term describing LLMs as statistical sequence predictors that string words together without true understanding. It named one side of the field's deepest running argument about what these systems actually do.

lenses.body: A quick, informal gut-feeling test of whether a new AI seems good, just by trying it out with a few questions, instead of running a real, careful test.
A legitimate, common practice worth naming accurately in coverage of a model release: informal spot-testing by early users often surfaces real issues before formal benchmark results are published.

A genuine complement to formal benchmarks rather than a replacement for them: informal testing can catch real regressions or oddities in a new model release that structured leaderboard metrics miss entirely, which is why experienced practitioners do both.

terms.example: Practitioners running favorite test prompts within hours of a launch.
terms.definition: An informal, subjective assessment of a model's quality from a few personal prompts. Common on release day, and a genuine complement to benchmarks: vibes catch regressions that leaderboards miss.

lenses.body: Building software by just telling an AI what you want in plain words and mostly trusting what it gives back, without checking every line carefully. Fine for a quick experiment, risky for something that really needs to work.

Worth distinguishing in coverage between prototyping use, which is broadly reasonable, and production use, which carries real risk; conflating the two misrepresents both the appeal and the danger of the practice.

Productive for rapid prototyping where mistakes are cheap to discover and fix, and genuinely hazardous for production systems where an unreviewed error can cause real harm; the term's half-affectionate tone reflects this real ambiguity about when the practice is appropriate.

terms.origin: Coined by Andrej Karpathy, February 2025.
terms.example: Building a working app through conversation without reading the generated code.
terms.definition: Programming by describing what you want in plain language to an AI assistant, accepting its output largely on trust. Productive for prototypes, hazardous for production, and named half-affectionately for that ambiguity.

lenses.body: Low-quality work made by AI that gets handed off to a coworker, who then has to spend time fixing it. It does not remove the work, it just pushes it onto someone else.

A useful, precise term for a real and underreported workplace dynamic: worth investigating in any story about AI productivity claims, since apparent individual efficiency gains can mask a net productivity loss once downstream correction time is counted.

Shifts effort downstream rather than eliminating it, which is the specific mechanism by which it can make a team measurably less productive even while the person generating the initial output feels more productive, since their own effort dropped while a colleague's rose.

terms.example: A machine-drafted report whose cleanup takes longer than writing it would have.
terms.definition: Low-quality AI-generated work product passed to colleagues who must then fix it. It shifts effort downstream instead of removing it, and it is the office-place face of the slop problem.

lenses.body: A product that is mostly just a nice-looking front door to someone else's AI, without adding much extra value of its own. People sometimes dismiss a product by calling it "just a wrapper."

A legitimate diligence question worth asking any AI startup: what specifically prevents the underlying model provider, or a well-resourced competitor, from replicating this product's interface in a weekend. A vague answer supports the "just a wrapper" concern.

The dismissal names a real structural concern: a thin interface over a third-party model has little defensibility if the underlying model provider can replicate the interface or a competitor can build an equivalent one quickly, since the actual value creation sits with the model owner.

terms.example: A startup whose entire product is one prompt in front of someone else's API.
terms.definition: A product that is a thin interface over a third-party model with little added value. The dismissal "just a GPT wrapper" names the investor concern: no moat between the product and the model it resells.

lenses.body: A shared set of rules that let one company's AI helper ask a different company's AI helper to do part of a job, the way two people from different companies can still work together on a project if they agree on how to communicate.

Cross-company agent delegation introduces a genuinely new trust boundary: your agent is now potentially accepting instructions or handing off tasks to an agent you do not control, which needs its own risk review distinct from internal multi-agent systems.

The inter-company layer of the agent stack, as MCP is the agent-to-tool layer; building against this standard rather than a custom integration means your agent can delegate to any A2A-compliant agent from another vendor, not just ones you specifically integrated with.

Worth understanding as the plumbing that will let your AI agents work with a partner or vendor's AI agents without custom integration for each relationship; an emerging standard here, similar to how email standards let any two companies exchange messages.

terms.origin: Google, April 2025; donated to the Linux Foundation.
terms.example: A procurement agent negotiating delivery windows with a supplier's agent.
terms.definition: An open protocol for interoperability between agents from different vendors, letting one organization's agent delegate to another's. The inter-company layer of the agent stack, as MCP is the agent-to-tool layer.

lenses.body: A smarter way of looking things up where the AI decides for itself what to search for, checks if it found enough, and searches again if it needs more, instead of doing just one search and stopping no matter what it found.

It replaces single-pass lookup with iterative research, trading latency for answer quality; reserve this for queries genuinely complex enough to need multiple search rounds, since the added latency and cost are not worth paying for simple lookups a single retrieval pass handles fine.

Better answer quality on complex questions comes at a real cost in response time and compute; make sure this is deployed selectively for genuinely complex queries rather than universally, or you will be paying the latency and cost premium on simple questions that did not need it.

A vendor offering "agentic RAG" should be able to show you the actual quality improvement over simpler single-pass retrieval on your specific use case, since the added complexity and cost are only justified where the quality gain is real and measurable.

terms.example: An agent running three refined searches before drafting its answer.
terms.definition: Retrieval driven by an agent that decides what to search, when to search again, and when it has enough. It replaces single-pass lookup with iterative research, trading latency for answer quality.

lenses.body: A pattern where an AI does not just answer once, but plans, tries something, checks its own work, and improves it, going around that loop as many times as needed, instead of giving one answer and being done.

The insight that made agents work: the loop, not the model, produces the reliability; a capable model without this iterative plan-execute-reflect structure still tends to make single-pass mistakes, while the same model wrapped in a good agentic loop can catch and correct its own errors.

The reliability improvement from AI systems often comes as much from the surrounding process design, checking and refining work, as from the underlying model's raw capability; a good agentic workflow can make a decent model perform like a great one.

If an AI tool seems to give noticeably better results than a plain chatbot for a complex task, it is often because the tool has this kind of check-and-refine loop built in behind the scenes, not because it is using fundamentally smarter AI.

terms.example: A drafting loop of generate, self-review, and revise beating one-shot output.
terms.definition: Iterative design patterns where AI loops through planning, executing, reflecting, and refining rather than generating once. The insight that made agents work: the loop, not the model, produces the reliability.

lenses.body: A self-directed AI system that can look at its situation, make a plan, use tools, and take a series of actions to reach a goal, instead of just answering a single question and stopping.

Requires the same identity, access-control, and audit rigor you would apply to a new system integration or employee, since it acts with real permissions and can take consequential actions; do not treat agent deployment as a lighter-weight decision than a traditional system integration.

The deployment unit of the agentic era, and the reason identity, permissions, and audit design all need revisiting; treat each deployed agent the way you would treat a new service account or employee, with its own scoped identity, logged actions, and access review, not as just another API call.

A meaningfully different governance object than a simple AI feature; an agent takes actions with real consequences across multiple steps, which means the review and oversight process appropriate for a chatbot feature is usually not sufficient for an agent.

terms.example: An agent monitoring a mailbox, triaging requests, and filing the routine ones.
terms.definition: An autonomous system powered by an LLM that perceives its environment, plans, uses tools, and executes sequential actions toward a goal. The deployment unit of the agentic era, and the reason identity, permissions, and audit design all need revisiting.

lenses.body: Running a big pile of AI requests all at once, overnight or on a schedule, instead of one at a time right away, which is cheaper but means you have to wait for the results instead of getting them instantly.

The right mode for anything that can wait: nightly classification, bulk extraction, scheduled scoring; explicitly separate latency-sensitive interactive use cases from batchable ones in your architecture, since defaulting everything to real-time inference wastes money on workloads that genuinely did not need it.

A real, often underused cost lever: any AI workload that does not need an instant answer, like nightly report generation or bulk document classification, is usually cheaper run in batch mode, and it is worth asking your team whether that mode is actually being used where applicable.

If you have a task that does not need an immediate answer, like sorting through a backlog of documents overnight, ask whether your AI tool or vendor offers a batch processing option; it is often noticeably cheaper than paying for instant responses you do not actually need.

terms.example: A million documents classified overnight at half the per-token rate.
terms.definition: Processing many requests offline at reduced cost, trading latency for price. The right mode for anything that can wait: nightly classification, bulk extraction, scheduled scoring.

lenses.body: Cutting a long document up into smaller pieces before giving it to an AI, sized so each piece is useful on its own, similar to breaking a long book into chapters instead of handing someone the whole thing at once.

Chunk size and overlap quietly determine RAG quality: too small loses context, too large buries the answer. Tune this parameter empirically against your actual document types and query patterns rather than defaulting to a generic chunk size, since the right size varies meaningfully by content type.

A technical detail with real business impact worth being aware of: a document-search or Q&A feature performing poorly is often traceable to how documents were split into pieces before indexing, which is a fixable configuration issue, not a fundamental AI limitation.

If an AI tool that searches your documents keeps missing information you know is in there, or gives you fragments that lack context, the underlying document-splitting settings are a likely cause worth raising with whoever set up the tool.

terms.example: Tuning chunk boundaries so clauses are never split mid-thought.
terms.definition: Splitting documents into passages sized for embedding and retrieval. Chunk size and overlap quietly determine RAG quality: too small loses context, too large buries the answer.

lenses.body: The careful work of putting exactly the right information, tools, and instructions in front of an AI so it has everything it needs to answer well, thinking about the whole picture the AI sees, not just the one question you typed.

The successor concept to prompt engineering: the prompt is one input, the engineered context is the whole picture the model sees. Think in terms of everything assembled into context, retrieved documents, tool definitions, conversation history, system instructions, not just the literal user-typed prompt text.

A more accurate framing than "prompt engineering" for what actually determines AI system quality in production; a team focused only on wordsmithing prompts while ignoring what information and tools are actually available to the model is missing most of the real engineering work.

The overall quality of an AI tool's answers depends on much more than just how you phrase your question; what documents, tools, and background information the tool has access to matters just as much, which is worth understanding when troubleshooting a disappointing result.

terms.origin: Term popularized across the industry in 2025.
terms.example: Curating which documents, schemas, and history enter each request.
terms.definition: The discipline of assembling the right information, tools, and instructions into a model's context window. The successor concept to prompt engineering: the prompt is one input, the engineered context is the whole picture the model sees.

lenses.body: A technique that lets an AI serving system swap requests in and out of a batch as they arrive and finish, instead of waiting for one whole group of requests to completely finish before starting the next group, which keeps the expensive hardware busy and efficient.

It is how serving stacks keep GPUs saturated under mixed traffic; a naive fixed-batch serving approach leaves expensive accelerator hardware idle between batches, so continuous batching is a meaningful efficiency technique worth using in any production serving infrastructure with variable request patterns.

A serving infrastructure detail that directly affects your AI costs at scale; ask whether your inference provider or self-hosted stack uses this technique, since its absence can mean paying for idle, underutilized hardware capacity.

A vendor's inference infrastructure efficiency, including techniques like this one, directly affects their unit economics at scale; worth asking about specifically when evaluating an AI infrastructure company's cost structure and margin trajectory.

terms.example: Short and long requests sharing a batch without blocking each other.
terms.definition: A serving technique that adds and removes requests from a running batch dynamically instead of waiting for the batch to finish. It is how serving stacks keep GPUs saturated under mixed traffic.

lenses.body: A way of measuring how similar two pieces of information are to an AI, by comparing the direction they point in a kind of mathematical space, rather than how big or small the numbers are. Things pointing in a similar direction are considered similar in meaning.

The standard distance in vector search: small angle, similar meaning. Understand this as the default similarity metric most vector search and retrieval systems use, and know that other metrics (like Euclidean distance) exist and can behave differently, particularly with embeddings that vary substantially in magnitude.

A technical detail underneath any semantic search or document-retrieval AI feature; not something you need to configure directly, but understanding that "similarity" is computed mathematically, not judged the way a person would, helps explain occasional odd retrieval results.

Not something you need to think about directly, but it is the underlying math that lets an AI tool find documents "similar" to what you are asking about, even when the wording is completely different; that is why good semantic search feels almost magical compared to old-fashioned keyword search.

terms.example: Ranking retrieved passages by cosine score against the query embedding.
terms.definition: A metric measuring how similar two embeddings are by the angle between them, independent of magnitude. The standard distance in vector search: small angle, similar meaning.

lenses.body: The price charged for each small chunk of text an AI reads or writes. Writing a longer answer usually costs more than a shorter one, and the AI's answers, the output, often cost more per chunk than what you typed in, the input.

Output tokens typically cost several times input, which is why verbose models are expensive models; a model or prompt style that produces long, wordy answers is directly more expensive to run than one that answers concisely, which is a real cost lever worth managing, not just a style preference.

The primary unit economics lever for any AI product; ask specifically about input versus output token pricing and typical response length for the target use case, since output-heavy applications have meaningfully different cost structures than input-heavy ones.

If your AI tool bill is higher than expected, check whether you are getting unnecessarily long, verbose answers; asking for more concise responses, when that is all you actually need, can meaningfully reduce cost since output text typically costs more per unit than input text.

terms.example: A workload repriced after switching to a model with cheaper output tokens.
terms.definition: The unit price for input or output tokens, the primary lever of AI unit economics. Output tokens typically cost several times input, which is why verbose models are expensive models.

lenses.body: Running an AI directly on a device, like a phone or a camera, instead of sending information to a distant computer over the internet and waiting for an answer back. It is faster, keeps information private on the device, and still works without an internet connection.

Explicitly weigh the capability tradeoff of a smaller on-device model against the latency, privacy, and connectivity benefits before defaulting to a cloud API; for many bounded, well-defined tasks the tradeoff genuinely favors edge deployment.

Chosen for latency, privacy, and offline operation, at the price of model size; a smaller, less capable model running locally is often the right tradeoff for use cases where instant response, data privacy, or unreliable connectivity matter more than having access to the absolute most capable model available.

A company building genuinely differentiated edge AI capability, rather than a thin wrapper around a cloud API, has a real technical moat worth understanding in more depth, since on-device model optimization is a nontrivial and valuable engineering skill set.

terms.example: A camera flagging defects on-device with no network round trip.
terms.definition: Running models locally on devices rather than in the cloud: phones, cameras, industrial sensors. Chosen for latency, privacy, and offline operation, at the price of model size.

lenses.body: A way of turning words, pictures, or other information into a list of numbers that captures their meaning, so that things with similar meanings end up with similar number-lists, which lets a computer do math to figure out what is related to what.

The data structure that makes meaning computable, and the foundation under semantic search and RAG. Choice of embedding model significantly affects downstream retrieval quality, and a domain-specific embedding model often outperforms a general-purpose one for specialized content, worth testing explicitly rather than assuming.

The underlying technology that lets an AI search tool find conceptually related information even when the wording differs completely from your search terms; worth understanding at a high level since it is foundational to most modern document-search and recommendation AI features.

This is the underlying technology that lets an AI search tool understand what you mean, not just match your exact words; it is why searching for "how to cancel" can find a document titled "subscription termination process" even though they share no words.

terms.example: Sentences mapped to vectors so related ideas sit near each other.
terms.definition: A vector representation of data in high-dimensional space where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric distance. The data structure that makes meaning computable, and the foundation under semantic search and RAG.

lenses.body: An automatic testing system that checks an AI's answers against what a good answer should look like, run every time something changes, the same way software gets tested automatically before it ships, so problems get caught before real users see them.

The CI/CD of AI quality: without evals, every prompt edit and model update is a blind deploy. Build and maintain a real evaluation suite for any production AI feature; shipping prompt or model changes without automated evaluation against known test cases is the AI-era equivalent of deploying code with no tests.

Ask your team directly whether AI features have an automated evaluation suite before shipping changes; the absence of one means every update is effectively untested in production, which is a real and often underappreciated operational risk.

Ask a portfolio company with AI-dependent features whether they maintain an automated evaluation suite; its absence is a genuine engineering maturity red flag, since it means quality regressions from model or prompt changes are likely being caught by users rather than by testing.

terms.example: A suite gating releases on accuracy, format, and tone checks.
terms.definition: An automated test suite scoring model outputs against expectations, run on every change. The CI/CD of AI quality: without evals, every prompt edit and model update is a blind deploy.

lenses.body: A shared, central place that stores the specific pieces of information an AI uses to make decisions, making sure the exact same version of that information is used both when the AI is being trained and later when it is actually running for real, so nothing gets mismatched.

It solves the classic ML failure of training on one definition of a feature and serving another; training-serving skew, where a feature is computed slightly differently between training and production, is a notoriously hard-to-debug source of production model underperformance that this architecture specifically addresses.

A infrastructure investment that pays off specifically when you have multiple predictive AI models sharing common input data; worth asking about if your organization has several machine learning models in production, since inconsistent feature definitions across them are a real and often invisible source of unreliable results.

Training-serving skew remains a persistent practical failure mode even with feature store infrastructure in place, since it addresses consistency of the stored feature values but not necessarily consistency of the computation logic generating them upstream, which requires additional discipline.

terms.example: Customer-tenure features computed once, consumed by every model consistently.
terms.definition: A central repository of curated model input features, serving the same values to training and production. It solves the classic ML failure of training on one definition of a feature and serving another.

lenses.body: A way of counting how much raw computing work went into training an AI, basically counting up all the individual math operations. This number has gotten so important that some new AI safety laws actually use it to decide which rules apply to which AI models.

Track and report training compute in FLOPs for any significant training run, both for internal capacity planning and because this figure is increasingly required for regulatory compliance documentation under emerging AI governance frameworks.

Training compute measured in FLOPs has become a regulatory trigger: thresholds in AI rules are written in these units; know where your organization's AI development or usage sits relative to any applicable regulatory compute thresholds, since crossing one can trigger new compliance obligations.

The choice of FLOPs as a regulatory threshold unit reflects an attempt to define capability tiers objectively and measurably, though the relationship between raw compute and actual downstream risk or capability remains an imperfect proxy worth ongoing scrutiny as training efficiency improves over time.

terms.example: A training run sized in FLOPs to check whether reporting thresholds apply.
terms.definition: Floating point operations, the standard unit of computation. Training compute measured in FLOPs has become a regulatory trigger: thresholds in AI rules are written in these units.

lenses.body: A specific file format used for storing AI models that have been shrunk down to run efficiently on regular computers, widely used by popular tools that let people run AI models on their own laptop instead of through a company's online service.

The de facto packaging standard of the local-model world; if distributing or downloading a model intended for local, self-hosted use with common tools like llama.cpp, this is the format you will encounter and need to work with as a practical default.

If you or a technical team member are exploring running an AI model directly on your own computer for privacy or cost reasons rather than through an online service, this is the common file format you will likely encounter for that kind of setup.

terms.origin: From the llama.cpp project, 2023.
terms.example: Downloading a GGUF quantization sized to fit a laptop's memory.
terms.definition: The file format for quantized local model weights used by llama.cpp and its ecosystem. The de facto packaging standard of the local-model world.

lenses.body: A carefully checked set of example questions with verified correct answers, used to test whether an AI is actually working well before it gets released. Since everything gets measured against this set, how good and accurate this set itself is puts a ceiling on how trustworthy the whole testing process is.

The quality anchor of an AI system: everything is measured against it, so its own quality is the ceiling. Invest real effort in curating and periodically reviewing your golden dataset, since a flawed or outdated evaluation set will produce misleadingly confident quality signals for every subsequent test run against it.

Ask specifically how your golden dataset was created and how recently it was reviewed before trusting a reported quality metric derived from it; a stale or poorly constructed evaluation set can make a genuinely degrading system look fine on paper.

Golden dataset construction methodology, including how representative it actually is of real production traffic distribution, is often underreported relative to the emphasis placed on the resulting evaluation scores, which is a genuine gap worth flagging when assessing the credibility of a reported benchmark result.

terms.example: Fifty expert-verified cases deciding whether a change ships.
terms.definition: A curated set of inputs with verified correct outputs, used for evaluation and release gating. The quality anchor of an AI system: everything is measured against it, so its own quality is the ceiling.

lenses.body: A special kind of computer chip originally built for video game graphics, that turns out to be really good at the kind of math AI training and running needs, since it can do huge numbers of simple calculations all at the same time.

GPU memory (VRAM) and compute capability, not just raw chip count, determine what model sizes and batch sizes are actually feasible; check specific hardware specifications against your model's requirements rather than assuming any GPU will work.

Its supply, price, and allocation shape the industry's strategy as much as any algorithm; access to sufficient GPU capacity, not just algorithmic capability, is a genuine competitive and strategic constraint for any organization doing significant AI training or high-volume inference.

GPU access and cost structure is a material factor in any AI company's unit economics and growth trajectory; ask specifically about compute procurement strategy, reserved capacity versus spot pricing, and how GPU costs scale with usage growth.

terms.example: H100-class accelerators anchoring both training clusters and serving fleets.
terms.definition: Hardware optimized for parallel matrix multiplication, the workhorse of deep learning training and inference. Its supply, price, and allocation shape the industry's strategy as much as any algorithm.

lenses.body: A way of looking things up that follows connections between related facts, like following a trail of linked dots, instead of just finding text that sounds similar to your question. This lets it answer questions that need chaining several connected facts together.

It answers the multi-hop questions vector search fumbles; worth adopting specifically for query types that require chaining several relational facts together, since standard vector-similarity retrieval genuinely struggles with this pattern regardless of how good the underlying embedding model is.

Worth investigating if your AI document-search or Q&A system struggles with questions that require connecting several related pieces of information; this is a specific, known limitation of standard retrieval approaches with a specific, known architectural fix.

The construction cost of building and maintaining an accurate knowledge graph from unstructured source documents remains a real practical barrier to adoption, and automated knowledge graph extraction quality directly bounds how well this retrieval approach can actually perform.

terms.origin: Microsoft Research, 2024.
terms.example: Tracing ownership across three linked entities to answer one query.
terms.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation over a knowledge graph rather than flat text chunks, following relationships instead of similarity alone. It answers the multi-hop questions vector search fumbles.

lenses.body: A special, fast kind of memory chip stacked right next to AI processing chips, feeding them data quickly enough to keep up with all their calculating. There is a real shortage of this specific kind of memory, which limits how many AI chips can actually get built.

A useful piece of context for understanding why certain accelerator configurations are priced or allocated the way they are; HBM capacity per chip is a hard physical constraint that directly limits model size and batch size feasible on a given piece of hardware.

The key supply constraint of the AI hardware market: accelerator output is bounded by HBM production; this specific component, not just general chip manufacturing capacity, is currently a genuine bottleneck worth understanding when assessing AI hardware availability and pricing trends.

A useful, more specific supply-chain fact than general "chip shortage" narratives: HBM production capacity specifically, dominated by a small number of memory manufacturers, is a real bottleneck worth tracking when evaluating AI infrastructure and hardware company prospects.

terms.example: Datacenter GPU availability tracking HBM manufacturing capacity.
terms.definition: Stacked memory placed on AI accelerators, feeding data fast enough to keep the compute busy. The key supply constraint of the AI hardware market: accelerator output is bounded by HBM production.

lenses.body: Combining two different ways of searching, one that matches exact words and one that understands general meaning, and blending their results together, because each method catches important things the other one misses.

Production best practice because each method catches what the other misses: exact identifiers and paraphrased meaning; do not rely on pure vector search alone for production retrieval, since it can miss exact-match queries like product codes or specific names that keyword search handles more reliably.

If your AI search tool sometimes misses exact terms like a specific product code or reference number even though it handles conceptual questions well, that is a known limitation of pure semantic search; ask whether a hybrid approach combining keyword matching is being used.

If an AI search tool struggles to find something when you search for an exact code, name, or reference number, even though it handles vague questions well, that is a known limitation worth mentioning to whoever manages the tool; combining it with regular keyword search usually fixes this.

terms.example: Part numbers found by keyword, related issues found by embedding, one result list.
terms.definition: Combining keyword and vector retrieval, then merging the ranked results. Production best practice because each method catches what the other misses: exact identifiers and paraphrased meaning.

lenses.body: Training is when a computer studies. Inference is the exam: it stops learning and just answers. Every time you ask a chatbot something, you are paying for the exam, not the studying.

The serving phase, and it behaves unlike training. Generation is autoregressive, one token at a time, and the KV cache grows as it goes, so throughput is usually bounded by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic. That is why batching, paging and cache management dominate serving performance, and why time-to-first-token and inter-token latency are measured separately.

The recurring cost of running a model, as opposed to the one-time cost of building it. Training is a capital event; inference is an operating expense that scales with usage, which means a successful product increases this bill rather than amortising it. Budget it as unit economics per request, not as a project cost.

The margin question for any AI company. Training spend is visible and finite; inference spend recurs with every user interaction and rises with adoption. Ask what a company pays per thousand requests, whether that figure is falling, and whether it owns, reserves or rents the capacity, because the answer determines whether growth improves or erodes gross margin.

terms.example: A deployed model answering user prompts around the clock.
terms.definition: The live execution phase where a trained model processes inputs and produces outputs. Training happens once; inference happens forever, which is why inference economics dominate production cost.

lenses.body: The web address where a hosted AI model actually lives and answers requests, the "front door" that every question sent to that AI, whether from a real user or someone trying to attack it, has to pass through.

Treat every inference endpoint as a security-relevant attack surface requiring authentication, rate limiting, input validation, and monitoring, the same as any other production API; it is the literal front door through which prompt injection and abuse attempts arrive.

Also a security-relevant surface: it is the front door through which every prompt, benign or hostile, arrives. Apply the same security rigor to this endpoint as any other production API surface, since it is genuinely the single point through which all model interaction, legitimate and adversarial, occurs.

This is the technical connection point your AI-powered product actually talks to; if you are working with a developer building an AI feature, it is worth confirming this connection is properly secured, the same as you would for any other sensitive piece of your online systems.

terms.example: A production endpoint with authentication, rate limits, and logging.
terms.definition: A hosted model behind an API, the deployment unit of model serving. Also a security-relevant surface: it is the front door through which every prompt, benign or hostile, arrives.

lenses.body: The whole set of techniques used to make running an AI cheaper or faster, without changing what it actually does. These small improvements added together often decide whether a business idea using AI is actually financially workable.

Layer multiple optimization techniques, batching, caching, quantization, together rather than relying on just one; they are generally complementary, and the combined effect on cost and latency is often substantial enough to change what is economically feasible to build.

The discipline that decides whether an AI feature's unit economics work; a feature that seems financially unviable at naive, unoptimized serving cost may be entirely workable once proper inference optimization is applied, which is worth investigating before abandoning an otherwise promising idea on cost grounds alone.

A meaningful differentiator between AI companies with genuinely sustainable unit economics and those without; ask specifically what inference optimization techniques a company employs, since the gap between naive and optimized serving cost can be the difference between a viable and unviable business model.

terms.example: A latency budget met through caching and a quantized model.
terms.definition: Techniques that lower serving cost or latency: batching, caching, quantization, distillation. The discipline that decides whether an AI feature's unit economics work.

lenses.body: The high-speed wiring that connects thousands of AI chips together so they can work as one giant machine during training. At a large enough scale, how fast the chips can talk to each other actually matters more than how fast each individual chip can calculate.

If planning or evaluating a multi-node training setup, interconnect bandwidth between nodes is often the actual bottleneck rather than per-chip compute; benchmark and plan around this explicitly rather than assuming more chips linearly translates to proportionally faster training.

At scale, training speed is bounded by how fast chips can talk, not how fast they compute; this is a real and often overlooked reason why simply buying more or faster individual chips does not proportionally improve training speed at very large scale, without matching interconnect investment.

A less visible but genuinely important infrastructure cost and differentiator for any company running large-scale training; interconnect quality is a real factor in effective training throughput that a simple chip-count comparison between competitors misses entirely.

terms.example: A cluster design where network topology sets the training throughput.
terms.definition: The high-speed links joining accelerators into a training cluster, NVLink within nodes, InfiniBand between them. At scale, training speed is bounded by how fast chips can talk, not how fast they compute.

lenses.body: The AI's working notes on everything it has already generated in the current conversation, kept in memory so it does not have to redo all that thinking from scratch for every new word. This is a big reason why long conversations use up a lot of memory.

Memory footprint of the KV cache is often the actual bottleneck limiting how many concurrent requests a given amount of GPU memory can serve, more so than the model weights themselves for long-context workloads; techniques like paged attention specifically address this constraint.

It is why long contexts consume memory: the cache grows with every token held; a service with long conversation history or large document context genuinely costs more to run per request, since memory usage, and therefore serving cost, scales directly with how much context the model is retaining.

A company's serving cost structure for long-context or long-conversation AI products depends heavily on how well they manage this specific memory constraint; ask whether they use modern techniques like paged attention, since naive KV cache management can make long-context features disproportionately expensive to serve.

terms.example: Serving memory sized by context length times concurrent sessions.
terms.definition: The stored attention states from tokens already processed, letting generation continue without recomputing the past. It is why long contexts consume memory: the cache grows with every token held.

lenses.body: How long you have to wait between asking an AI something and getting an answer back. AI that is technically very smart but painfully slow to respond can still feel disappointing to actually use, because waiting a long time makes it feel less impressive.

Measure and optimize both time-to-first-token and total completion time separately, since they affect perceived responsiveness differently; a slow start with fast streaming afterward can feel better to users than a fast start followed by a long wait for completion.

The user-experience number: perceived intelligence degrades quickly when it arrives slowly; a highly capable but slow-responding AI feature often performs worse in real user satisfaction than a somewhat less capable but faster one, which is worth weighing explicitly against raw benchmark capability when choosing a model for a user-facing feature.

If customers or your team find an AI tool frustrating despite it giving good answers, check how long it actually takes to respond; slow response time genuinely affects how useful and pleasant a tool feels to use, independent of the actual answer quality.

terms.example: A chat product targeting sub-second time to first token.
terms.definition: The delay between sending a prompt and receiving a response, measured to first token and to completion. The user-experience number: perceived intelligence degrades quickly when it arrives slowly.

lenses.body: Using one AI to grade the answers given by another AI, following a specific set of grading rules, which lets you check huge numbers of answers automatically instead of needing people to read and grade every single one by hand.

Powerful and biased: judges prefer verbose, confident answers, so the rubric and spot-checks carry the integrity. Regularly spot-check the judge model's scoring against genuine human judgment, since documented biases toward longer, more confident-sounding answers can systematically skew automated evaluation results if left unchecked.

A genuinely useful technique for scaling quality evaluation past what human review capacity allows, but ask what validation exists confirming the judge model's scoring actually tracks genuine quality rather than just favoring longer or more confident-sounding answers.

Documented judge-model biases, including length bias and confidence bias, are well-characterized in the literature, and mitigating them through careful rubric design, randomized answer ordering, and periodic human calibration checks remains an active and genuinely important area of evaluation methodology research.

terms.example: Ten thousand outputs graded overnight against a five-point rubric.
terms.definition: Using a model to grade another model's outputs against a rubric, scaling evaluation past what humans can score. Powerful and biased: judges prefer verbose, confident answers, so the rubric and spot-checks carry the integrity.

lenses.body: All the practical, ongoing work of running AI systems in the real world: keeping track of prompts, testing quality, watching what is happening, and controlling costs, similar to how regular software needs ongoing maintenance and monitoring after it is built.

Invest in proper tooling for prompt versioning, evaluation, tracing, and cost monitoring from early on, rather than retrofitting it after problems emerge in production; the operational surface area of an LLM-based system is genuinely larger than traditional software and needs corresponding tooling.

MLOps extended to systems whose behavior changes with a prompt edit; a small, seemingly minor prompt change can have outsized effects on system behavior in a way traditional software changes usually do not, which is why this operational discipline deserves its own dedicated attention rather than being treated as an afterthought to deployment.

A company's LLMOps maturity, prompt versioning discipline, evaluation infrastructure, cost monitoring, is a meaningful and often underexamined signal of overall engineering maturity for any AI-dependent business; worth asking about directly in diligence.

terms.example: A release pipeline covering prompts, models, and eval gates together.
terms.definition: The operational practice for deploying, monitoring, and improving LLM applications: prompt management, evals, tracing, cost control. MLOps extended to systems whose behavior changes with a prompt edit.

lenses.body: An AI model you download and run yourself on your own computer, instead of sending your questions over the internet to a company's servers. It usually is not quite as capable as the biggest online AI, but it is more private and does not need an internet connection.

Test capability gap between your intended local model and the equivalent cloud frontier model explicitly on your actual task before committing; the gap varies significantly by task type and has narrowed considerably for many bounded use cases, but is still real for genuinely open-ended tasks.

Chosen for privacy, cost, and independence, priced in capability against frontier APIs; worth genuinely evaluating for use cases involving sensitive data or requiring offline operation, understanding you are trading some capability ceiling for those real and sometimes decisive benefits.

A company building genuine local-model capability, rather than simply wrapping a cloud API, has real differentiated technical work worth understanding, particularly for use cases in privacy-sensitive or connectivity-constrained industries where this is a genuine, defensible advantage.

terms.example: A firm running an open-weights model on premises for sensitive documents.
terms.definition: A model downloaded and run on hardware you control, via tools like Ollama and llama.cpp. Chosen for privacy, cost, and independence, priced in capability against frontier APIs.

lenses.body: The set of practices for keeping AI models running well after they have been built and deployed: tracking versions, watching for problems, and knowing how to retrain or roll back when something starts going wrong, the same kind of ongoing care regular software needs after launch.

Build in model performance monitoring and a defined retraining or rollback process from the start, not as an afterthought; models degrade silently as real-world data distribution shifts, and without active monitoring this degradation can go unnoticed for a long time.

CI/CD discipline applied to artifacts that degrade as the world changes; unlike traditional software, which mostly stays correct until someone changes the code, a machine learning model can silently degrade in accuracy as real-world data drifts away from what it was trained on, which is exactly what this discipline exists to monitor and catch.

A company's MLOps maturity, having real versioning, monitoring, and retraining processes rather than a one-time model deployment, is a genuine signal of whether their AI-dependent product will remain reliable over time as real-world conditions inevitably shift.

terms.example: A retraining pipeline triggered by drift monitoring.
terms.definition: The practices for deploying and maintaining machine learning models in production: versioning, monitoring, retraining, rollback. CI/CD discipline applied to artifacts that degrade as the world changes.

lenses.body: A single control point that all requests to different AI companies' models pass through, letting a company keep track of what is being used, enforce rules, and log everything in one place, instead of connecting to each AI provider separately with no central oversight.

A meaningful security and governance control point worth implementing if your organization uses multiple AI providers; centralizing model access lets you enforce consistent data handling policy, apply redaction of sensitive information, and maintain a single audit log across otherwise disparate integrations.

The central governance point of an AI stack: one place to route, meter, redact, and audit every model call; if your organization uses multiple AI providers, this gives you one central place to enforce policy and get visibility, rather than trying to govern each integration separately, which tends to become unmanageable at scale.

A company offering a model gateway as a product is solving a real, growing enterprise pain point, multi-vendor AI governance, as organizations increasingly use several different AI providers and need centralized policy enforcement and visibility across them.

terms.example: All model traffic flowing through a gateway that logs and rate-limits it.
terms.definition: A proxy providing one interface, logging, and policy enforcement across multiple model providers. The central governance point of an AI stack: one place to route, meter, redact, and audit every model call.

lenses.body: A smart traffic-director that sends each request to whichever AI model can handle it for the lowest cost, only using a bigger, more expensive AI when the request actually turns out to need it. Most requests are simple, so most requests should be cheap.

Worth implementing for any application with a meaningful volume of simple, routine requests mixed with occasional complex ones; a well-tuned router can substantially cut cost with minimal quality impact, though the routing logic itself, deciding what counts as "simple," needs careful design and testing.

Cost optimization as architecture: most requests are easy, and easy should be cheap; using the most capable, most expensive model for every single request, regardless of complexity, is usually wasteful, and a well-designed routing layer can substantially reduce cost without a corresponding drop in overall answer quality.

A meaningful cost-optimization lever worth asking any AI-dependent company about; a company routing every request to its most expensive available model, rather than intelligently escalating only when needed, likely has real headroom to improve margins through better routing architecture.

terms.example: Routine queries to a small model, hard ones escalated to the frontier.
terms.definition: A layer that sends each request to the cheapest model able to handle it, escalating only when needed. Cost optimization as architecture: most requests are easy, and easy should be cheap.

lenses.body: A special chip built into modern phones and computers specifically designed to run AI calculations efficiently, using much less battery power than running the same AI on the device's regular main processor.

Check whether your target device has a capable NPU and whether your model or framework can actually take advantage of it before assuming on-device inference will be efficient; not all local model runtimes are optimized to use NPU hardware effectively yet, which varies by platform.

The hardware basis of the AI PC and on-device assistant wave; understand this as the enabling hardware trend behind the current push toward on-device AI features in consumer devices, which matters for evaluating whether a "local AI" product claim is genuinely differentiated or hardware-dependent marketing.

Hardware differentiation in the NPU space is a genuine competitive factor among device manufacturers currently racing to support on-device AI features; worth tracking specifically when evaluating consumer hardware companies positioning around AI capability.

terms.example: A laptop running local transcription on its NPU without waking the fans.
terms.definition: A dedicated accelerator for neural network math built into consumer devices. The hardware basis of the AI PC and on-device assistant wave.

lenses.body: Keeping detailed records of exactly what an AI system was asked, what information it looked up, what it answered, and how much it cost, so when something goes wrong you can actually investigate and understand why, instead of just guessing.

Build in comprehensive tracing and logging from the start for any production AI system, capturing prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and cost per request; retrofitting observability after a production issue has already occurred is far harder than building it in from the beginning.

The difference between debugging a system and guessing at one; without this kind of detailed tracing and logging, diagnosing why an AI system produced a bad or unexpected result becomes genuinely difficult, and "we are not sure why it did that" becomes a recurring and costly answer.

If a developer builds an AI feature for your business, ask whether they have set up proper logging that lets them see exactly what happened when something goes wrong; without it, diagnosing a problem later becomes much harder and slower.

terms.example: A trace showing exactly which retrieved chunk produced a wrong answer.
terms.definition: Tracing, logging, and metrics for AI application behavior: what was asked, what was retrieved, what was answered, at what cost. The difference between debugging a system and guessing at one.

lenses.body: Running an AI model completely on your own device, with your information never being sent anywhere else over the internet at all, which is the strongest form of privacy protection for AI use, though it is limited by how much memory and battery power your specific device has.

The strongest available data-residency and privacy guarantee for AI use, since data genuinely never leaves the device; worth mandating specifically for the most sensitive use cases where even a vendor's zero-data-retention promise is not sufficient assurance.

The privacy-preserving and offline-capable deployment mode, bounded by device memory and power; worth prioritizing specifically for use cases involving genuinely sensitive data where sending information to any external server, even a secure one, is unacceptable, understanding the capability tradeoff that comes with device hardware constraints.

If you handle particularly sensitive customer or business information, an AI tool that runs entirely on-device, rather than sending data to an online service, offers a genuinely stronger privacy guarantee, worth specifically asking about if privacy is a top priority for a given use case.

terms.example: Dictation processed on the phone, usable in airplane mode.
terms.definition: Executing a model entirely on local hardware, with data never leaving the device. The privacy-preserving and offline-capable deployment mode, bounded by device memory and power.

lenses.body: A clever memory-management trick for AI serving, borrowed from how computer operating systems handle memory, that stores an AI's working notes in flexible chunks instead of one solid block, which wastes much less memory and lets a server handle far more requests at once.

It cut serving memory waste dramatically and underpins modern high-throughput inference engines; if self-hosting model serving infrastructure, use an inference engine that implements this technique, since the memory efficiency gain translates directly into meaningfully higher request throughput on the same hardware.

A behind-the-scenes technical improvement that directly affects how much AI serving capacity you get from a given amount of hardware; worth confirming your inference provider or self-hosted stack uses modern techniques like this one, since the efficiency gain is substantial.

The operating-system-memory-paging analogy underlying this technique is a strong example of applying decades-old systems engineering principles to a new domain, and it has become a foundational technique that essentially all modern high-throughput inference serving engines now implement in some form.

terms.origin: Introduced with vLLM, 2023.
terms.example: A serving stack fitting far more concurrent sessions in the same GPU memory.
terms.definition: A memory-management method storing the KV cache in non-contiguous blocks, the way operating systems page memory. It cut serving memory waste dramatically and underpins modern high-throughput inference engines.

lenses.body: A system where an AI first looks up relevant, real, current information from a specific set of documents before answering, instead of relying only on what it memorized during training, so its answers can reflect up-to-date or private company information and can show exactly where each fact came from.

The default enterprise pattern: it grounds answers, enables citations, and keeps knowledge updatable without retraining; this is specifically what lets an AI system reflect your company's current, private information accurately, and it is far cheaper to keep updated than retraining a model, since you just update the underlying documents.

A well-implemented RAG architecture is often what actually differentiates an enterprise AI product from a thin wrapper around a general model; ask specifically about retrieval quality, chunking strategy, and citation accuracy, since these implementation details substantially affect real product quality.

This is the technology that lets an AI tool actually know your specific business information, your documents, policies, and data, rather than only knowing general facts from its original training. Ask any AI vendor whether and how they implement this if you need answers grounded in your own information.

terms.origin: Lewis et al., 2020.
terms.example: A document QA system answering from the company's own files, with sources.
terms.definition: An architecture that retrieves relevant context from external data sources before the model generates, so answers reflect current, private, or specialized information. The default enterprise pattern: it grounds answers, enables citations, and keeps knowledge updatable without retraining.

lenses.body: A cap on how many requests or how much text an AI account is allowed to send in a given amount of time, which protects against a runaway AI process accidentally sending an enormous, expensive flood of requests all at once.
