Demand forecasting, credit scoring, and churn prediction are mature predictive-AI applications that predate the current generative wave by years, which means predictive AI is likely already embedded in existing operations, forecasting, scoring, planning, well before any recent AI initiative, and it is worth taking that existing use into account before assuming generative AI is an organization's first real AI deployment.

Predictive AI is also generally easier to evaluate rigorously than generative AI, since forecasts can be checked against actual outcomes with standard statistical methods rather than requiring the harder, less settled evaluation approaches generative systems need. For a genuinely forecasting-shaped problem, that measurability makes predictive AI often the simpler and more measurable choice, distinct from whatever attention generative AI is currently drawing.

This data does not cover specific predictive AI techniques or algorithms, how predictive and generative AI are typically combined in a single system, or revenue figures for predictive versus generative AI applications.

/ai-glossary/self-critique/.body:
Self-critique has the model review its own answer against criteria before finalizing, the draft-then-revise pattern: a second pass catches what the first pass, committed token by token, could not, shown by a model checking its summary against the source before submitting a final version.

That description of the first pass, committed token by token, names the specific limitation self-critique addresses. Because generation happens sequentially without the ability to revise earlier tokens once they are written, an explicit review-and-revise step can catch errors that the original generation process structurally could not fix on its own, the same way a person rereading their own writing catches errors that slipped past while first writing it in one direction.

The technique is relatively cheap for what it buys: explicitly prompting a model to review its own draft against stated criteria before finalizing often catches errors that a single-pass generation misses, at the cost of one additional inference call, which is a modest price for a meaningful quality improvement. Anyone using an AI tool can apply the same idea directly by asking it to review and critique its own answer against specific criteria before accepting the result, a simple extra step that often catches mistakes or gaps the first answer missed.

This data does not cover how self-critique compares in effectiveness to Reflexion-style multi-round critique loops, or what fraction of errors a single critique pass typically catches.

/ai-glossary/stop-sequence/.body:
A stop sequence is a string that halts generation the moment it is produced, the blunt, reliable way to prevent runaway completions and keep output inside expected boundaries, such as generation ending cleanly at a closing tag rather than continuing past it.

Its bluntness is a design feature, not a limitation. Unlike more nuanced controls, a stop sequence is a hard, unconditional cutoff the moment the specified string appears, which makes it simple and predictable but not adjustable mid-generation, a tradeoff that suits its actual purpose: enforcing a structural boundary rather than shaping content within that boundary.

That structural-boundary role is what makes it particularly useful for preventing a model from continuing past a defined output format into unwanted additional commentary or explanation, a specific and common failure mode where a model finishes the requested content but keeps generating unrequested extra text afterward. Most consumer AI tools do not expose this control directly, but more technical AI platforms let a developer set specific stopping points precisely to address a response that consistently runs on with unwanted extra content.

This data does not cover how stop sequences are technically implemented across different model APIs, or how they interact with structured output formats like JSON mode.

/ai-glossary/system-prompt/.body:
A system prompt is the high-level instructions provided before user interaction that define the model's role, boundaries, and context, the governing document of a deployment, and a favorite target of injection attacks for the same reason, shown by a support bot's system prompt fixing scope, tone, and escalation rules before any user message arrives.

That dual identity, governing document and attack target, follows directly from the same underlying fact. Because the system prompt defines the model's core rules and boundaries for an entire deployment, an attacker who can override or extract it has effectively compromised the whole system's intended behavior, which is exactly why it needs to be treated as a security-critical component rather than a configuration detail.

The practical consequence is that a system prompt should be defended against extraction and override attempts, and its contents should never be assumed to stay confidential from a sufficiently determined adversarial user. It is also the reason two different AI-powered products built on the same underlying model can behave very differently: the company building each product has set hidden rules and a role for the model before a user ever starts typing, which shapes its whole personality and boundaries in ways the underlying model alone does not determine.

This data does not cover specific system prompt extraction or override techniques, or best practices for defending a system prompt against adversarial users.

/ai-glossary/time-to-value/.body:
Time to value is the elapsed time from project start to measurable business benefit, a key portfolio filter: two projects with equal returns are not equal if one pays back in a quarter and the other in two years, shown by prioritizing the document-automation project that shows returns within one quarter over a slower alternative.

That inequality between equal-return projects is the whole point of tracking this metric separately from total return. A faster payback frees capital and builds organizational confidence sooner, which has real value beyond the eventual total return figure, since a project that pays back quickly can be reinvested or expanded while a slower one is still absorbing capital with nothing yet to show for it.

For anyone evaluating an AI initiative from the outside, time to value alongside total expected return gives a more complete picture than ROI alone, since a long payback period carries real opportunity cost and execution risk that a headline ROI figure does not capture on its own. Favoring projects that show a real benefit quickly over ones promising a bigger payoff far in the future also has a practical benefit beyond the value itself: faster feedback allows course-correction before too much has been spent on an approach that turns out not to work.

This data does not cover how time to value is typically measured or defined precisely, or how it should be weighted against total return when comparing very different projects.

/ai-glossary/tool-registry/.body:
A tool registry is the catalog of tools, with their schemas and permissions, that an agent is allowed to call, the practical control surface for agent blast radius: an agent cannot misuse a tool it was never granted, shown by a registry granting a finance agent report-generation tools but not payment execution.

That framing, control surface for blast radius, is precise rather than a loose metaphor. An agent literally cannot misuse a tool that is not in its registry, which means the registry itself, not the agent's judgment or any downstream check, is what actually bounds what a compromised or misbehaving agent could do, keeping it minimal and task-specific is a direct limit on worst-case outcomes rather than a best-practice preference.

That directness is what makes the registry a genuinely useful accountability artifact after an incident. The documented tool registry for an agentic system shows precisely what the system was permitted to do, which supports an accountability claim after an incident far better than a general description of intended behavior, since the registry is an enforced technical boundary rather than a stated intention. Treating it the same way an access-control list would be treated, reviewed on a schedule, with unused entries removed and a change-control process required before adding a new tool, especially one with write access or financial consequences, follows directly from how much the registry actually determines.

This data does not cover how tool registries are typically implemented technically, or how permission scoping within a single tool entry is usually structured.

/ai-glossary/vector-search/.body:
Vector search retrieves records by embedding similarity rather than keyword match, the lookup that finds meaning: documents about the topic, whether or not they share the words, shown by a semantic lookup surfacing a relevant memo that a keyword search missed entirely.

The canonical example makes the mechanism concrete: a search for "how do I stop my subscription" can successfully find a document titled "cancellation instructions" even though the two share almost no identical words, because vector search matches on what the query and the document mean, not on the literal characters they contain, which is a fundamentally different matching criterion than keyword overlap.

That conceptual strength is why it is a meaningful upgrade over older keyword-only search technology for most knowledge-retrieval use cases, finding conceptually relevant information regardless of exact wording overlap. It is also why pairing it with keyword search in a hybrid approach is standard for production systems, since pure vector search can occasionally miss exact-match needs like specific codes or names that a paraphrase-tolerant search is not optimized to catch precisely, the same complementary weakness that motivates hybrid search generally.

This data does not cover how vector similarity is computed technically, what embedding models are typically used, or how vector search indexing scales to very large document collections.

/ai-glossary/agent-boundary/.body:
An agent boundary is the documented limit on what an agent may read, write, and trigger, and the data's core claim is procedural: writing the boundary down is the control itself, since an undocumented boundary cannot be audited.

That claim reframes what counts as a finding during review. In a boundary matrix, a grid showing each agent's permitted data sources, write targets, and downstream actions, an empty cell is not a gap in the paperwork, it is itself the finding, because it means nobody has established or reviewed what that agent is or is not permitted to do in that category. The data's example is a matrix where every blank cell is explained rather than left silent.

That standard applies regardless of how well an agent appears to behave. The data states that any agent without an explicit, current boundary document should be treated as unreviewed, whatever its actual track record looks like, because good behavior observed so far is not the same as a documented limit on what it is allowed to do.

For regulated review, a documented boundary also functions as evidence: it shows precisely what a system was permitted to do at the time it was deployed, which is useful in an incident review or conformity assessment. The data does not describe how boundaries should be enforced technically, only that documenting them is itself the control, and undocumented boundaries do not qualify as reviewed regardless of behavior.

/ai-glossary/autonomy-level/.body:
Autonomy level is how far an agent may act before a human must confirm, ranging from suggest-only through approve-to-execute to fully autonomous, and the data treats setting this deliberately, per task, as one of the core agent governance decisions, not a default to leave unexamined.

That per-task granularity is the data's specific recommendation. A coding agent might warrant approve-to-execute for a deploy but suggest-only for a database schema change, since hardcoding one autonomy level for an entire agent ignores that different actions carry very different risk. An agent allowed to draft emails freely but required to get approval before sending is the data's example of one system operating at two different autonomy levels for two different actions.

For governance purposes, the data recommends mapping autonomy level directly to a documented risk tier per action type, and treating any change to that level, especially raising it, through the same change-control process used for a permissions escalation for a human user, since expanding what an agent can do without confirmation is functionally the same kind of event.

The data does not specify how many autonomy levels a governance framework should define or how to assess risk tier for a novel action type. It establishes why the level must be set per action rather than per system, and why raising it deserves the same scrutiny as a human permissions change, not a complete risk-tiering methodology.

/ai-glossary/chatgpt-moment/.body:
A ChatGPT moment is the point at which a technology suddenly reaches mass public awareness, named for November 2022, and the data notes drily that every emerging field now markets itself as awaiting its own.

That naming convention is precise about what it actually describes. The data is specific that the term refers to sudden, mass public awareness, not gradual adoption, a distinct kind of adoption curve, slow buildup followed by sudden mass attention, rather than steady growth over time. Robotics investors forecasting the sector's ChatGPT moment is the data's example of the phrase being applied predictively to a different field.

For anyone evaluating such a claim, the data recommends using the term precisely: a technology claiming to be having its ChatGPT moment is making a specific and checkable claim about attention, not capability, so the two should not be conflated when the phrase gets used in coverage or marketing.

The data does not describe what conditions actually produce a moment of sudden mass awareness or predict which fields are likely to have one. It establishes what the term specifically claims and where it originated, not a forecasting tool for identifying the next one. It comes from the launch of ChatGPT, November 30, 2022.

/ai-glossary/context-recall/.body:
Context recall measures whether retrieval fetched everything needed to answer the question, and the data notes a specific methodological requirement that sets it apart from other evaluation metrics: unlike faithfulness and answer relevance it generally requires ground truth, since something must define what should have been retrieved.

That ground-truth dependency is what lets it catch a specific failure the data says other metrics miss: a confident, well-grounded answer built on half the evidence. The data's example makes this concrete: a legal answer scoring high on faithfulness while context recall sits at 0.62 because the retriever consistently missed the second governing statute, an answer that is faithful to what it retrieved while still being incomplete, since faithfulness only checks consistency with what was actually fetched, not whether enough was fetched.

That distinction is the metric's core value: a system can score well on every metric that checks the answer against its retrieved evidence while still failing silently because the evidence itself was incomplete, and context recall is specifically what surfaces that gap.

The data does not describe how the ground truth needed for scoring is established or what recall score should be treated as acceptable for a given use case. It establishes what failure the metric uniquely catches and why it requires ground truth to compute, not a scoring standard. It is a core Ragas retrieval metric.

/ai-glossary/context-window/.body:
A context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can process and retain during a single interaction, its working memory, and the data is direct about what this constrains: everything the model should consider, instructions, documents, history, must fit inside it.

That fitting requirement is where practical problems arise. A 200 thousand token window holding an entire contract set for review is the data's example of a large window used at scale, but the data also flags a specific failure mode: silent truncation of older content when the window fills up, described as a common, hard-to-debug production issue if not actively tracked. For developers, the recommendation is to know a model's actual context window size and monitor how close a given request comes to it, since truncation happens without an explicit error.

For a user noticing an AI seeming to forget something discussed earlier in a long conversation or large document, the data frames this as a likely consequence of the window filling up and older material being dropped, not a mistake in the ordinary sense, since once accumulated content exceeds the limit, older material typically gets dropped or truncated.

The data does not specify how truncation is handled by different systems, whether from the start, the middle, or some other policy. It establishes what the window constrains and why forgetting is a structural consequence of exceeding it, not a truncation policy comparison.

/ai-glossary/cost-per-token/.body:
Cost per token is the unit price for input or output tokens, the primary lever of AI unit economics, and the data states the asymmetry plainly: output tokens typically cost several times input, which is why verbose models are expensive models.

That asymmetry has a direct operational consequence: a model or prompt style that produces long, wordy answers is more expensive to run than one that answers concisely, a real cost lever worth managing rather than merely a style preference. A workload repriced after switching to a model with cheaper output tokens is the data's example of this cost structure being acted on directly.

For evaluating an AI product's economics, the data recommends asking specifically about input versus output token pricing and typical response length for the target use case, since output-heavy applications carry meaningfully different cost structures than input-heavy ones. For a user facing a higher-than-expected bill, the data's specific suggestion is checking whether responses are unnecessarily long and asking for more concise output when that is all that is actually needed.

The data does not give specific pricing figures or compare cost structures across providers. It establishes the input-output cost asymmetry and its direct consequence for verbosity, not a pricing table.

/ai-glossary/data-readiness/.body:
Data readiness is whether the information an AI use case relies on is reliable enough for the task, accurate, current, consistent, and owned, and the data is specific about what closing this gap actually requires: practical internal controls, not a data science team or enterprise warehouse.

That practical framing matters because it changes what the fix looks like. A pricing use case paused because three spreadsheets disagreed on the current rates is the data's example of a readiness failure, and the data states most data readiness gaps are fixable operational problems, inconsistent naming, stale records, unclear ownership, not infrastructure problems requiring major investment.

For a company reporting strong AI results, the data treats unreliable underlying data as a foundation that will eventually surface as an incident, recommending a specific question before crediting an AI performance claim: how was data quality validated. For any AI task deemed important, the data recommends checking whether the underlying information it relies on, customer records, inventory, pricing, is actually accurate and current first, since garbage data produces confidently wrong AI answers regardless of how capable the model itself is.

The data does not provide a checklist for assessing data readiness or specify what level of consistency counts as sufficient for a given use case. It establishes why the fix is usually operational rather than technical, not a readiness assessment methodology.

/ai-glossary/data-residency/.body:
Data residency is the requirement that data be stored and processed within a specific jurisdiction, and the data states its practical effect directly: it constrains model and provider choice, since a capability that only runs in another region is a capability the regulated workload cannot use.

That constraint operates regardless of how good the model itself is. Choosing an EU-region deployment to keep customer data inside the jurisdiction is the data's example of the decision this requirement forces, a provider selected specifically for where it processes data, not only for its underlying capability. A capability that only runs in a data center outside the required jurisdiction is, per the data, simply unusable for that regulated workload, whatever its quality.

For evaluating a company's AI stack, the data recommends checking whether it was chosen with this constraint in mind or retrofitted after the fact, since a company operating under strict residency requirements has a narrower vendor selection than one without. For anyone handling data subject to residency requirements, healthcare or financial information among the examples, the data recommends checking specifically where a vendor actually processes and stores data, not just where the vendor company is headquartered.

The data does not list which jurisdictions impose residency requirements or specify how compliance is technically verified. It establishes why residency narrows vendor choice directly, not a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction compliance guide.

/ai-glossary/double-descent/.body:
Double descent is test error rising and then falling again as model size or training time grows past the interpolation point, and the data states directly what this overturned: it contradicted classical bias-variance intuition and helped explain why enormous models generalize.

That contradiction is specific: the traditional statistical expectation was that a model complex enough to perfectly fit its training data would generalize poorly, but double descent showed that pushing well past that point can actually restore and improve generalization. Performance recovering as a model grows past the classical overfitting peak is the data's example of this counterintuitive recovery in practice.

For a developer making scaling decisions, the data's practical warning is not to assume test performance will monotonically worsen as model complexity increases past the point of fitting training data perfectly, since the empirical reality is more nuanced than classical intuition suggests, which is directly relevant to decisions about model scaling.

The data notes the underlying theory is still being worked out: the theoretical explanation for double descent, connecting to implicit regularization effects of gradient descent in overparameterized regimes, remains an active area of theoretical machine learning research, with several competing but not fully unified explanatory frameworks. The data does not resolve which explanatory framework is correct or specify at what scale the second descent typically begins. It establishes why the phenomenon overturned an old assumption and that its theory remains unsettled, not a settled explanation. It comes from Belkin et al., 2019, with a deep learning demonstration by Nakkiran et al.

/ai-glossary/frontier-model/.body:
A frontier model is one at or near the current maximum of capability, typically the largest and most recently released systems, and the designation now carries real regulatory weight: frontier status increasingly triggers evaluation and reporting obligations, illustrated by a new flagship release undergoing pre-deployment safety evaluation before it ships.

That regulatory weight is what separates this term from ordinary marketing language about a model being cutting-edge. In some jurisdictions, being labeled a frontier model brings specific, formal evaluation and reporting requirements under emerging AI regulation, which makes frontier status a legal and compliance category as much as a capability claim.

For anyone building on a frontier-designated model, that classification often comes bundled with usage restrictions or evaluation obligations attached by the provider or a regulator, so the terms of use and any reporting duties are worth checking before building critical infrastructure on top of one. For a buyer, a vendor's frontier-model status is a compliance fact worth understanding on its own terms, not just a proxy for how capable the system is.

This data does not name which jurisdictions currently impose frontier-model obligations, what evaluation a frontier designation specifically requires, or how the threshold for frontier status is set.

/ai-glossary/golden-dataset/.body:
A golden dataset is a ceiling, not just a test: every quality metric an AI system reports is measured against it, so the dataset's own accuracy and coverage set the upper bound on how trustworthy any of those metrics can be, no evaluation can be more reliable than the reference it is checked against.

That ceiling is easy to miss because attention gravitates to the resulting scores rather than to how the dataset itself was built. The gap named here is specific: how a golden dataset was constructed, and how representative it actually is of real production traffic, tends to be reported far less than the benchmark numbers it produces, which is a real reason to be skeptical of a quality claim before checking its source. A stale or poorly constructed evaluation set can make a genuinely degrading system look fine on paper, so periodic review of the dataset itself, not just the scores, is part of maintaining it honestly.

What is not given is a specific method for building or auditing a golden dataset, or a minimum size; the one example offered is fifty expert-verified cases used as a release gate, which is illustrative of scale rather than a prescribed number. A team adopting this practice has to define its own construction and review process.

/ai-glossary/llm-as-a-judge/.body:
LLM as a judge uses one model to grade another model's outputs against a rubric, scaling evaluation past what humans can score, illustrated by ten thousand outputs graded overnight against a five-point rubric, and it is powerful and biased at once: judges prefer verbose, confident answers, so the rubric and spot-checks carry the actual integrity of the result.

That bias is well-characterized rather than speculative. Documented judge-model biases toward longer, more confident-sounding answers can systematically skew automated evaluation results if left unchecked, which means the technique's usefulness at scale comes bundled with a specific, known failure mode rather than being a neutral substitute for human judgment.

The practical response is validation, not abandonment. Regularly spot-checking the judge model's scoring against genuine human judgment, alongside careful rubric design and randomized answer ordering, is how the length and confidence biases get caught before they distort results. For anyone relying on this technique, the honest question is what validation confirms the judge's scoring actually tracks genuine quality rather than just favoring longer or more confident-sounding answers, since the technique's speed advantage does not by itself establish its accuracy.

This data does not cover specific rubric design methods, how large the length and confidence biases typically are, or how judge-model scores compare to human agreement rates numerically.

/ai-glossary/meta-prompting/.body:
Meta prompting uses a model to write or refine prompts for itself or another model, industrializing prompt engineering: the optimization loop runs in software instead of in someone's head, run in practice as a pipeline that iterates a prompt against an eval set until scores plateau.

That shift from manual to automated iteration is the core change. Rather than a person manually trying different phrasings through trial and error, the refinement process itself becomes something a model can help automate and systematize, generating variations, catching ambiguities, or suggesting improvements to an existing prompt faster than a person iterating by hand.

The technique scales down to individual use as easily as it scales up to a pipeline. Anyone struggling to get good results from an AI tool can directly ask the AI itself to help write a better prompt for the task, which often works surprisingly well and skips much of the manual trial and error. At the system level, it is worth building into any application maintaining many prompts, since an automated eval-driven loop can converge on improvements faster than manual iteration across a large prompt library.

This data does not cover how eval sets used in meta-prompting pipelines are constructed, or how meta-prompted results compare in quality to prompts written entirely by hand.

/ai-glossary/model-artifact/.body:
A model artifact is the weights, adapters, and tuning data that constitute a trained model, a production asset with recovery requirements: losing it can mean losing a capability no backup of the surrounding code can restore, which is why disaster-recovery inventories now include model weights and adapters with defined restore objectives.

That framing, a production asset rather than just another file, is the point. Standard software recovery processes typically do not account for these large, specialized files, and treating a trained model as just another item in a general backup process risks losing a capability that took significant time and money to originally produce, since the code around the model is recoverable in a way the trained weights themselves are not.

For anyone responsible for AI infrastructure, model artifacts need their own dedicated backup and recovery procedure, distinct from standard code and infrastructure backups. For anyone evaluating a company's AI capability from the outside, trained model weights represent real, embedded capital investment, which makes backup, recovery, and access control practices for these artifacts a genuine business continuity and IP question, not just a technical detail.

This data does not cover typical model artifact sizes, specific backup technologies used for them, or how access control for model weights is usually implemented.

/ai-glossary/model-whiplash/.body:
Model whiplash is the disruption caused by frequent model version changes altering behavior mid-production, and it breaks tuned prompts and calibrated workflows, which is why version pinning exists, illustrated by a prompt suite failing overnight after a silent model upgrade nobody on the receiving end requested.

The disruption is structural rather than incidental: a prompt carefully tuned against one version's specific behavior has no guarantee of working the same way against a later version, since the model that changed sits underneath the application rather than inside it, invisible to the code that depends on its exact behavior. That invisibility is what makes the failure feel sudden even though the underlying cause, a provider-side version change, happened somewhere else entirely.

Version pinning, locking a deployment to a known model version, exists as a direct practice-level response to this specific disruption, protecting a workflow from exactly the kind of unannounced change that breaks tuned prompts. For any AI-dependent business, whether that pinning strategy exists is a fair operational question, and its absence is a real vulnerability rather than a hypothetical one, since the failure mode has a documented mechanism rather than being speculative.

This data does not cover how often model providers typically change versions, what pinning options different providers offer, or how long a pinned version typically remains supported.

/ai-glossary/prompt-caching/.body:
Prompt caching makes a repeated prefix of a prompt, a long system instruction or a shared document, nearly free to reuse after the first call, and the data's point is that this changes how production prompts get structured, not just what they cost.

The practical implication is architectural. Stable, reusable content such as system instructions and reference documents belongs first in a prompt, with variable per-request content placed after it, so the cacheable portion stays consistent across calls. The data gives a concrete case, a fifty page policy document cached once and reused across thousands of queries, to show the scale at which this matters.

For any application with high call volume and repeated context, this is presented as a real cost and latency lever, not a minor optimization. The data frames it as significant enough to be worth checking for specifically when an AI bill is a meaningful expense.

What the data does not cover is how caching is priced or how long a cached prefix remains valid before it expires. It establishes the mechanism and the architectural response to it, not the operational details of managing a cache.

/ai-glossary/regularization/.body:
Regularization is the family of techniques that discourage overfitting, dropout, weight decay, early stopping, data augmentation, collectively the discipline of making models learn structure instead of noise, shown by weight decay and early stopping steadying a small-data fine-tune that would otherwise memorize its limited examples.

The various individual techniques within this toolbox all address the same underlying overfitting problem from different angles, which is why they are usefully grouped together conceptually even though they operate quite differently in mechanism, one constraining weight magnitude, another stopping training early, another expanding the effective training set. Applying multiple techniques together rather than relying on just one is standard practice in most well-tuned training pipelines, since weight decay, early stopping, and data augmentation are often complementary rather than redundant.

The role of explicit regularization changes at scale, though. The relative importance of these techniques diminishes at the massive data scale used in modern LLM pretraining, since abundant, diverse data provides substantial implicit regularization on its own, which is part of why some techniques standard in earlier, smaller-scale deep learning are used more sparingly in current large-scale training, not because the underlying overfitting problem disappeared but because scale itself supplies some of what explicit regularization used to provide.

This data does not cover the mathematical mechanics of specific regularization techniques, how implicit regularization from data scale is measured, or optimal regularization strength for a given dataset size.

/ai-glossary/role-prompting/.body:
Role prompting assigns the model a persona or professional role to shape tone, depth, and vocabulary, and it works because register lives in the training data: "as a forensic accountant" summons different priors than "as a friend," shown by a prompt opening "You are an experienced auditor" to sharpen skepticism in the response.

That mechanism, register living in the training data, is why the technique works at all rather than being a superficial trick. The model has learned statistical associations between certain roles and certain vocabulary, tone, and depth of explanation from the huge volume of text it was trained on, so naming a role summons those learned associations directly, shifting output style without needing to spell out every stylistic preference explicitly.

The technique is cheap and effective for tone specifically, but its reach has a boundary worth knowing. Role alone usually shapes style more reliably than it shapes structure, which means combining it with more specific format instructions gets better results than relying on role assignment by itself for anything requiring a particular output structure. For quick, low-effort improvement, though, simply asking an AI to act as a specific kind of professional, a marketing expert or a customer service specialist, often noticeably improves the tone and relevance of its answer for that kind of task.

This data does not cover how role prompting interacts with more structured prompting techniques, or which roles tend to produce the strongest tonal shifts.

/ai-glossary/sloppification/.body:
Sloppification is the gradual degradation of a content platform by mass-generated material, and search results and stock imagery were the early casualties, with every open submission surface a candidate, shown by a stock-photo site overrun by synthetic images of uneven quality.

The reason every open submission surface is a candidate, not just the platforms already affected, is structural: any platform accepting open submissions is a structural candidate for the same degradation over time as generation cost approaches zero, since the underlying enabling condition, cheap AI content generation at volume, applies equally to any surface that accepts public or user submissions, not only the specific ones documented so far.

That structural framing is what makes this a trackable, reportable phenomenon rather than an anecdotal complaint. It is worth investigating quantitatively where possible, such as the share of new listings, images, or reviews that appear machine-generated over time, since the degradation this term describes is a measurable trend on a given platform rather than a vague impression, and a rising share of that kind of content over time is direct evidence of the process actually occurring.

This data does not cover specific measured sloppification rates on any named platform, or what interventions have proven effective at slowing the process.

/ai-glossary/acceptance-rate/.body:
Acceptance rate measures how often users actually keep an AI tool's suggestions rather than ignoring them, and the data's central claim is that it is a leading indicator, a falling rate signals eroding trust before overall usage numbers drop.

That timing gap is the reason it matters more than raw usage. A team could still be logging in and generating suggestions while quietly accepting fewer and fewer of them, and usage counts alone would not show that decline until much later, once people have started working around the tool rather than through it. Tracking the fraction of code-completion suggestions developers accept is the data's concrete example of what this looks like in practice.

For evaluating a vendor's tool from outside, the data treats acceptance rate as harder to game than a login count or seat number, since it reflects an actual choice made suggestion by suggestion rather than mere presence in the software.

The data does not give a benchmark for what an acceptable rate looks like or how quickly a decline should trigger concern. It establishes the metric and why it leads other signals, not a threshold for reading it.

/ai-glossary/backpropagation/.body:
Backpropagation is the fundamental algorithm that calculates how much each weight contributed to the error, allowing neural networks to learn by adjusting weights in the right direction, and the data's plain statement of its reach is that every modern deep learning system trains on it.

That universality is worth taking literally. The reverse pass distributing blame for a wrong prediction across billions of weights is the data's description of the mechanism at the scale of current models, computing how error at the output should be attributed backward through each layer, the foundational mechanism underlying essentially all neural network training regardless of architecture.

Despite that dominance in practice, the data notes an unresolved question sitting alongside it: backpropagation's biological plausibility remains debated, and alternative credit-assignment mechanisms continue to be explored in computational neuroscience-adjacent research, even though backprop remains completely dominant in practical machine learning. Practically, the data also notes it is rarely implemented by hand today, since automatic differentiation in frameworks like PyTorch handles it, though understanding the underlying mechanism is described as essential for debugging training instabilities like vanishing or exploding gradients.

The data does not explain what specifically causes vanishing or exploding gradients or detail the alternative credit-assignment mechanisms being explored. It establishes why the algorithm is foundational and where genuine debate about it still exists, not a debugging guide or a comparison of alternatives. It dates to Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams, 1986.

/ai-glossary/batch-inference/.body:
Batch inference is processing many requests offline at reduced cost, trading latency for price, and the data frames it as the right mode for anything that can wait: nightly classification, bulk extraction, scheduled scoring.

The economics are concrete in the data's example: a million documents classified overnight at half the per-token rate, the specific tradeoff of accepting a delay in exchange for a substantially lower cost per unit of work. The data recommends explicitly separating latency-sensitive interactive use cases from batchable ones in system architecture, since defaulting everything to real-time inference wastes money on workloads that genuinely did not need an instant answer.

For evaluating whether an organization is capturing this savings, the data frames it as a real, often underused cost lever, worth specifically asking whether batch mode is being used wherever a workload does not need an instant answer, such as nightly report generation or bulk document classification, rather than assuming everything already runs at the cheapest available rate.

The data does not specify typical latency for batch jobs beyond overnight, or compare batch discounts across providers. It establishes the core tradeoff, latency for price, and the kinds of workloads that should use it, not a pricing comparison.

/ai-glossary/cold-start-data/.body:
Cold start data is a small seed dataset used to bootstrap a training stage before larger-scale methods take over, and the data's metaphor for it is precise: the starter culture of a pipeline, tiny, curated, and disproportionately influential.

That disproportionate influence is the practical concern. Seed reasoning traces stabilizing a model before reinforcement learning is the data's example of what cold start data does in practice, shaping the initial direction that a larger-scale training method then builds on. Because the small seed dataset shapes that initial direction, its quality has an outsized effect on the final outcome relative to its actual size, which is why the data recommends investing disproportionate quality control effort into cold start data relative to its size, since errors or biases introduced here can compound and be amplified through the subsequent larger-scale stage.

The data notes this area is comparatively underexplored: the specific composition and quality requirements for effective cold start data, and how they differ across different downstream training methods, remains somewhat underexplored compared to the extensive literature on large-scale pretraining data curation.

The data does not specify how large a cold start dataset typically needs to be or what quality criteria distinguish an effective one. It establishes why its small size does not mean small importance, not a curation standard.

/ai-glossary/cross-attention/.body:
Cross-attention is attention where the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another, letting one stream consult a second, and the data names two concrete places this happens: it is how a decoder reads an encoder, and how an image generator reads a text prompt.

The key structural difference from self-attention is specific: queries come from one sequence while keys and values come from a different sequence entirely, one stream consulting another rather than attending only to its own prior content. A text prompt steering an image diffusion model through cross-attention layers is the data's example of this mechanism directly shaping output.

That same mechanism doubles as a debugging tool. Cross-attention maps can be visualized to see which prompt tokens actually influenced which regions of a generated image, which the data calls genuinely useful specifically for diagnosing why a text-to-image model ignored part of a prompt. The data notes this visualization has become a standard interpretability tool for such failures, though whether attention weight actually reflects causal influence remains a live methodological question.

The data does not detail how attention maps are computed or resolve the causal-influence question it raises. It establishes what cross-attention structurally does and its diagnostic use, not a settled account of what the visualized weights actually mean.

/ai-glossary/data-provenance/.body:
Data provenance is a verified record of where data came from and what it may be used for, and the data states directly why this matters for AI specifically: consent, licensing, and residency obligations travel with the data into every model that touches it, so provenance is what makes a training set defensible rather than merely available.

That defensible-versus-available distinction is the practical risk. Tracing a fine-tuning dataset back to its licensed sources before a customer audit asks is the data's example of provenance functioning as intended, verification completed before it is demanded rather than scrambled together after. The data is explicit that data being technically accessible does not mean its use for AI training was legally authorized, and calls this gap a real and growing source of litigation.

For approving a custom model training initiative, the data recommends asking specifically about data provenance, not just data availability, since the two are treated as genuinely separate questions with different risk profiles. For security and compliance functions, the recommendation is to maintain provenance documentation as a first-class artifact alongside a data inventory, since the associated obligations travel with the data into every downstream system that touches it, trained models included.

The data does not describe what specific documentation constitutes adequate provenance evidence or how disputes over licensing are typically resolved. It establishes why provenance is now a distinct legal exposure from mere data access, not a compliance checklist.

/ai-glossary/deflection-rate/.body:
Deflection rate is the share of support contacts fully resolved without a human, and the data names it the core support-AI metric while flagging exactly how it gets gamed: deflection that leaves problems unresolved returns as escalation and churn.

That gaming risk is the data's central warning. A support bot resolving six of ten contacts end to end, measured by no-reopen rates, is the data's example of measuring the metric correctly, closure defined by the problem staying solved rather than by the conversation simply ending. The data states directly that a high deflection rate paired with rising churn is a warning sign, not a win, since solving a problem badly and having it come back later does not really count as success.

For evaluating a vendor's reported deflection number, the data recommends asking for it alongside downstream churn and re-contact rate, not in isolation, since a vendor reporting an impressive standalone deflection number without those companion metrics may be reporting a gamed statistic. The same caution applies at any scale: tracking not just how many support questions an AI handles alone but whether those customers come back with the same problem later is what actually distinguishes closing tickets from solving problems.

The data does not specify what deflection rate is typical or good for a given industry, or describe how no-reopen windows should be measured. It establishes why the raw number can mislead and what companion metrics correct for that, not a benchmark figure.

/ai-glossary/detector-bypass/.body:
Detector bypass is editing AI text to evade automated AI-writing detectors, and the data names the specific problem this creates: an academic integrity flashpoint made worse by the detectors' unreliability, since they flag honest work and miss edited machine work in both directions.

That bidirectional unreliability is the data's central concern, not the bypass technique itself. A paraphrasing pass defeating a plagiarism-style AI detector is the data's example of the bypass side, while the data notes the opposite failure occurs just as seriously: honest human writing gets falsely flagged as AI-generated, undermining trust in the detection process on both sides of the question.

For reporting or acting on an AI-detection accusation, the data recommends caution specifically because these detectors have documented false-positive rates against genuine human writing, meaning a tool's output alone is not reliable evidence of anything, in either direction.

The data does not report specific false-positive or false-negative rates for named detection tools, or describe alternative approaches to verifying AI-generated text. It establishes why the technology is unreliable in both directions and why that undermines trust in the whole process, not a resolution to the underlying detection problem.

/ai-glossary/diffusion-model/.body:
A diffusion model is a class of generative models that create data by learning to reverse a noising process, iteratively removing noise until an image, video, or audio sample emerges, and the data states the source of its output quality precisely: quality comes from many small denoising steps rather than one leap.

That many-small-steps design is what the data credits for the technique's rise: this iterative refinement approach is what let diffusion models overtake GANs as the dominant image-generation paradigm, trading generation speed for more stable training and higher output diversity. Stable Diffusion and Midjourney generating images from text prompts is the data's example of the technique deployed at scale.

The data notes a direct engineering tradeoff inside the technique itself: the number of denoising steps is a direct, tunable tradeoff between generation quality and speed, and production applications typically use distilled or accelerated samplers to reduce steps needed, since the naive many-step process is too slow for interactive use.

Theoretically, the data connects diffusion models to a broader research thread: the theoretical connection between diffusion models and score-based generative modeling, learning the gradient of the data distribution, unified what were initially separate research threads and continues to inform new sampler and training-objective designs.

The data does not specify how many denoising steps production systems typically use or compare specific distillation techniques. It establishes why the iterative approach displaced GANs and what tradeoff it requires for real-time use, not an implementation guide. It comes from Ho et al., 2020, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.

/ai-glossary/encoder-decoder/.body:
Encoder-decoder is an architecture pairing an encoder for the input with a decoder for the output, and the data names its natural fit precisely: the shape for tasks that transform one sequence into another, with translation and summarization its home ground before decoder-only models absorbed most tasks.

That historical displacement is specific and qualified: the natural fit is for tasks that clearly transform one full sequence into a different full sequence, though decoder-only architectures have proven flexible enough to handle these tasks too, meaning the older architecture was not proven wrong so much as made less necessary by a more flexible alternative. T5 translating or summarizing by encoding the source and decoding the target is the data's example of the architecture applied to its original home ground.

The data notes it remains a reasonable choice in specific circumstances: still a reasonable architecture choice for well-defined sequence-to-sequence tasks with a fixed input and output structure, like machine translation, where the explicit separation can offer training efficiency advantages over a general decoder-only approach.

Research continues comparing the two: the relative advantages of encoder-decoder versus decoder-only architectures for sequence transformation tasks remain an area of ongoing comparison, with encoder-decoder models sometimes showing better sample efficiency on tasks with clear input-output structure despite decoder-only models' broader current adoption.

The data does not quantify the sample-efficiency advantage or specify which sequence-to-sequence tasks benefit most from the explicit encoder-decoder split. It establishes why the architecture still has a place despite decoder-only's broader adoption, not a task-by-task recommendation.

/ai-glossary/flash-attention/.body:
Flash Attention's core contribution is algorithmic: same mathematical operation, reorganized to minimize GPU memory traffic, which directly enabled the long context windows that define current large language models.

The innovation matters because transformer attention is memory-bound, not compute-bound. Moving data between GPU memory and compute cores costs more time and energy than the actual floating-point operations. Flash Attention restructures the computation to keep intermediate values in faster cache rather than writing them to main memory and reading them back. This is not a mathematical shortcut or approximation. It produces identical results to standard attention while reducing both memory bandwidth and often wall-clock runtime. The effect compounds across longer contexts, where naive attention becomes prohibitively expensive.

For AI scaling, this exemplifies a constraint that raw compute power alone cannot solve. More GPUs or faster chips help little if the bottleneck is memory bandwidth between components. Flash Attention showed that careful algorithm design for hardware hierarchy, rather than inventing new mathematics or buying larger machines, could unlock capability at lower cost. The pattern has since informed kernel optimization across the field.

The data does not cover which models currently use Flash Attention, what fraction of the inference speed gain derives from memory reduction versus runtime improvement, or whether other memory-aware optimizations have since superseded it. It confirms the hardware-level insight but not its current deployment footprint.

/ai-glossary/greedy-decoding/.body:
Greedy decoding always selects the highest-probability next token, which makes it deterministic and fast, but the best next word at every single step rarely produces the best paragraph overall, so it is prone to repetitive, flat text, useful mainly for a deterministic compliance task where variation is unwanted.

The mechanism explains its own weakness: because greedy decoding never considers whether a slightly less probable word now might lead to a much better sentence later, it tends to produce text that is locally reasonable at each step but globally repetitive or flat across a full paragraph. Every choice is locally optimal and the overall output can still be worse than a less greedy strategy would have produced.

That tradeoff makes the technique, effectively temperature at or near zero, the right choice specifically when reproducible, deterministic output matters more than quality, such as testing or evaluation pipelines, and the wrong choice for creative or open-ended generation where flat, repetitive output is a real cost.

This data does not cover alternative decoding strategies like beam search or nucleus sampling, or how greedy decoding's determinism is measured against other low-temperature settings.

/ai-glossary/jagged-frontier/.body:
The jagged frontier names the uneven capability boundary where AI excels at some tasks and fails at adjacent, seemingly similar ones, coined in a 2023 Harvard Business School and BCG field study of consultant AI use, exemplified by a model acing complex analysis while fumbling a simple formatting request.

This unevenness explains inconsistent user experience directly, since a system can feel brilliant on one task and frustrating on a nearly identical one for reasons that are not obvious from the outside. Two seemingly similar tasks can sit on opposite sides of this boundary, which means capability does not generalize smoothly the way intuition suggests it should.

The practical consequence is that task-level piloting beats general intuition for deciding what to deploy. A company assuming capability generalizes smoothly across similar tasks is likely to be surprised by this unevenness once it hits production, which is why the useful question before deployment is whether a decision was based on testing the specific task or on a general capability assumption drawn from a different, similar-looking one.

This data does not cover what specifically predicts which side of the frontier a task falls on, or how the jagged frontier changes as models improve.

/ai-glossary/paged-attention/.body:
Paged attention reduced serving memory waste dramatically by storing the KV cache in non-contiguous blocks instead of requiring contiguous allocation, directly increasing how many concurrent requests a GPU can handle on the same hardware.

The technique borrows from operating systems, which have managed memory fragmentation for decades through paging. Applied to inference serving, it lets a GPU hold far more concurrent sessions because memory no longer gets wasted on unused reserved blocks. This matters for AI infrastructure because serving is increasingly the bottleneck. If inference engines waste memory, they waste the expensive compute they are supposed to utilize.

For anyone running or buying AI serving capacity, the efficiency gain translates directly into throughput per dollar of hardware. A serving stack that implements paged attention fits more requests into the same GPU memory, which means lower serving costs per inference and higher utilization of the buildings and power already committed to running models.

What this does not tell you is how much waste paged attention eliminates on your specific workload, which depends on sequence lengths and batch patterns. It also does not address the other constraints on serving throughput, like network bandwidth or the speed of token generation itself, which may be the actual bottleneck in your case.

/ai-glossary/personalization/.body:
Personalization adapts a system's output to an individual using their history, preferences, or context, and in AI systems this usually means retrieval over stored user data rather than a separate model trained for each person, illustrated by an assistant recalling a user's preferred report format from earlier sessions, held in a profile store.

That retrieval-based mechanism is exactly why personalization sits inside privacy scope rather than beside it. The personalization store is a record about the user, subject to retention schedules, access controls, and erasure requests like any other data about that person, since it is not a special category exempt from the ordinary rules governing personal data, it is personal data stored to make outputs more relevant.

The practical consequence is that a deletion request must reach the personalization store the same way it reaches any other system holding data about a user, which means personalization architecture and privacy compliance are the same design problem rather than two separate ones layered on top of each other. Treating the profile store as outside privacy scope because its purpose is customization rather than identification would be a category error against how the data is actually stored and used.

This data does not cover how personalization stores are typically structured, retention periods for stored preference data, or how personalization interacts with data portability requests.

/ai-glossary/pilot-purgatory/.body:
Pilot purgatory is the condition where AI pilots multiply but none reach production, the dominant enterprise failure mode, usually rooted in pilots designed to demonstrate rather than to integrate, exemplified by twelve proofs of concept and zero production deployments over two years running.

The root cause named here is specific rather than vague: pilots built to demonstrate a capability, to show that something is technically possible, do not automatically carry a path into an actual workflow, since demonstrating and integrating are different design goals that require different planning from the start. A pilot optimized for the demonstration goal can succeed at that goal completely while still having no route to production.

For an organization, the fix is designing every pilot with a defined path to production from the outset, since expecting one to stall here is the reasonable default absent that plan. For an outside observer, a high count of AI pilots paired with a low count of production deployments is a legitimate red flag worth probing directly, since it usually indicates the demonstration-versus-integration problem rather than predicting an eventual breakthrough once enough pilots accumulate.

This data does not cover what specifically differentiates a pilot designed for integration from one designed for demonstration, or typical pilot-to-production conversion rates.

/ai-glossary/prompt-chaining/.body:
Prompt chaining is the boundary case that defines what makes something a full agent: the steps are fixed by the designer in advance, and the moment a system starts choosing its own next step instead of following a preset sequence, it has crossed into agent territory.

The practical case for chaining over a full agent is simplicity: a chain is easier to debug and more predictable to run, because every step is known ahead of time. It remains the right choice whenever a task follows the same sequence every time, extract, then summarize, then format, and a team should only reach for the added complexity of a dynamic agent once the task genuinely requires the system to decide its own path rather than follow one.

What is not addressed here is where a chain breaks down: no failure mode is described for when one step's output does not cleanly match what the next step expects, and no guidance is given for how many steps a chain can hold before its rigidity becomes a liability rather than an asset. The entry establishes the boundary with agents, not the operational limits of chaining itself.

/ai-glossary/prompt-template/.body:
A prompt template's value is concentration: instead of quality work on a prompt scattering across every place in a codebase that happens to ask a similar question, it lives in one maintained artifact, and improving that one template improves every call site that uses it.

That concentration is what makes systematic testing feasible. A maintained library of templates for repeated tasks, rather than prompts written ad hoc inline throughout a codebase, is the practice recommended here, because testing and improving one artifact is tractable in a way that testing dozens of scattered, slightly different inline prompts is not. The same logic applies at smaller scale: any repeated question asked of an AI tool with small variations each time is a candidate for a reusable template with blanks for the parts that change.

What is not addressed is how a template should be versioned or how a team should measure whether a template change improved or degraded output across its many call sites; the entry describes why centralizing prompts helps, not the process for maintaining that central artifact over time.

/ai-glossary/reasoning-model/.body:
A reasoning model spends inference-time compute the way a bigger model spends training-time compute: both cost more, but a reasoning model pays that cost per query, deliberately, in exchange for working through a hard problem step by step rather than answering on the first pass.

That per-query cost is why routing matters more than model choice alone. The right architecture, according to the definition here, is a simpler and faster model on easy queries with a reasoning model reserved for genuinely hard, multi-step problems, since using a reasoning model on simple queries adds latency and cost without an accuracy benefit to show for it. This is a meaningfully different resource tradeoff than simply deploying a larger model everywhere: the class traces to OpenAI's o1 in September 2024.

What is not defined here is the line between "easy" and "hard" that should trigger routing to a reasoning model, or how much accuracy gain justifies the added latency for a given use case. The entry names the tradeoff and its origin, not a threshold for making the routing decision in practice.

/ai-glossary/semantic-search/.body:
Semantic search retrieves based on meaning rather than keyword overlap, implemented by comparing embeddings, and it finds the document that answers the question even when the question shares no words with it, such as a query for "reducing churn" surfacing a document titled "customer retention playbook."

That capability, finding an answer with no literal word overlap, is exactly what keyword-based search structurally lacks. The underlying mechanism compares numerical embeddings representing meaning rather than matching literal text strings, which is why two phrasings of the same underlying idea can be matched even when they share no vocabulary at all.

That conceptual strength comes with a specific, complementary weakness. Semantic search excels at conceptual matches but can sometimes miss exact-term precision that keyword search handles more reliably, like exact product codes or names, which is why combining semantic search with traditional keyword search in a hybrid approach is standard for most production retrieval systems rather than relying on semantic search alone. Embedding model choice also significantly affects semantic search quality in domain-specific applications, and general-purpose embedding models often underperform domain-fine-tuned alternatives on specialized vocabulary, a practical gap between benchmark performance and real deployment quality.

This data does not cover how embeddings are computed, specific embedding model comparisons, or how hybrid search architectures merge semantic and keyword results.

/ai-glossary/vector-database/.body:
A vector database is a database designed to store, index, and query high-dimensional embeddings efficiently for similarity search, the retrieval backbone of RAG systems, and a data store whose contents deserve the same protection as the documents they encode, capable of serving millions of document embeddings with millisecond lookups.

That last clause, same protection as the documents they encode, is a specific and consequential security claim rather than general caution. Embeddings are not as opaque or unrecoverable as they might intuitively seem, and under certain attack conditions they can be used to partially reconstruct information about the underlying content, which means treating a vector database as lower-risk than the source documents it was built from is a real security gap, not a reasonable simplification.

Applying the same access control, encryption, and audit logging standards to a vector database as would be applied to the original source documents follows directly from that fact, since the risk profile is closer to the original data than intuition about "just numbers" would suggest. For a business, this is also the specific technology underneath any AI feature that lets someone search across a large collection of documents by meaning rather than exact keyword matching, worth knowing by name when discussing AI search capability with a developer or vendor.

This data does not cover how embeddings can technically be partially reconstructed, specific vector database products or their security features, or how indexing techniques achieve millisecond-scale lookups at large scale.

/ai-glossary/agentic-workflow/.body:
The reliability gain from an AI agent typically comes from the loop, plan, execute, reflect, refine, repeat, not from a smarter underlying model, which is why the same model can look mediocre used once and capable used inside a good agentic workflow.

The mechanism is iteration with a check step built in. A single-pass answer has no chance to catch its own mistakes; a system that plans, tries something, checks its own work, and revises gets multiple chances to correct course before the output is final. That is a process design choice, not a capability upgrade to the model doing the work.

The consequence for evaluating AI tools is that apparent quality differences between a plain chatbot and an agentic tool often trace to this loop rather than to which model sits underneath. What the data here does not establish is how many iterations are enough, or when the loop stops improving output and starts wasting compute on diminishing returns; the entry names the mechanism, not its limits.

/ai-glossary/answer-relevance/.body:
Answer relevance measures whether a response actually addresses the question asked, independent of whether it is true, and the data's key distinction is that these are separate qualities: a response can be perfectly faithful to its sources and still evade the question, or bury the answer in unrequested detail.

That separation is illustrated concretely: asking for a filing deadline and receiving an accurate but rambling summary of the whole statute is described as high faithfulness paired with low answer relevance, an answer that is not wrong but also does not do what was asked. This shows why the two metrics need to be tracked separately rather than treating factual accuracy as sufficient on its own.

The data describes how the metric is typically scored: by generating candidate questions from the answer and measuring how closely they match the original question asked. A large mismatch between the generated questions and the original suggests the answer wandered from what was actually asked, even if every fact in it checks out.

The data does not specify a numeric threshold for what counts as acceptable answer relevance or compare it against other evaluation metrics beyond faithfulness. It establishes the distinction between relevance and accuracy and the scoring method used to measure it. It is one of the core Ragas metrics, and TruLens carries an equivalent feedback function.

/ai-glossary/confusion-matrix/.body:
A confusion matrix is a table of true and false positives and negatives that shows exactly how a classifier errs, not just how often, and the data states precisely where the useful information lives: the off-diagonal cells are where the operational story lives.

That distinction between error rate and error type is the practical point. Did the model call a cat a dog, or a dog a cat, are different problems even though both count as one wrong answer in a simple accuracy score. Discovering a model's errors concentrate in one costly direction is the data's example of what the off-diagonal cells reveal that a single accuracy number cannot.

The data draws a specific consequence from this: two systems can share the same accuracy score while making very different kinds of mistakes, so for a system whose error types carry different costs, like flagging a good customer as fraud versus missing real fraud, the recommendation is to ask for this breakdown before approving the system rather than relying on the headline number alone. For regulatory purposes, the data adds that aggregate accuracy alone does not show whether errors are evenly distributed across protected classes or concentrated in ways that raise a disparate-impact concern.

The data does not specify what off-diagonal pattern should trigger a specific remediation, or provide worked examples of disparate-impact analysis using the matrix. It establishes why error type matters more than error rate alone, not a remediation framework.

/ai-glossary/context-stuffing/.body:
Context stuffing is filling the context window with as much reference material as possible on the theory that more is better, and the data's finding runs directly against that theory: it often degrades precision, since relevance beats volume, and retrieval that selects usually outperforms context that hoards.

That degradation is concrete in the data's example: pasting nine documents when the two relevant ones would score higher, meaning the extra material is not neutral padding but something that can actively bury the useful content. The data recommends investing in retrieval quality, selecting the most relevant chunks, over simply maximizing how much context is provided, since a well-curated smaller context frequently outperforms a maximal, unfiltered one on both accuracy and cost.

For a user working directly with an AI tool, the data extends the same lesson: giving it only the specific, relevant material for the task at hand usually produces better results than pasting in everything available and hoping the tool figures out what matters, since more information is not automatically better.

The data does not specify how much irrelevant material typically starts degrading performance or describe how to measure relevance before including a document. It establishes why volume works against precision rather than for it, not a curation method.

/ai-glossary/deep-learning-dl/.body:
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning based on neural networks with many layers, which learn their own representations from raw data rather than relying on hand-built features, and the data names its reach directly: the engine behind image recognition, speech, and large language models.

That self-representation quality is the key distinction the data draws from earlier machine learning: deep networks learn their own useful representations from raw data rather than relying on hand-built features a person designed in advance, which is what let the same basic approach scale across images, speech, and text rather than needing a bespoke feature-design effort for each domain. A deep network learning edge, texture, and object concepts from pixels alone is the data's example of that self-learned representation in action.

The data notes a specific tradeoff that comes with this power: deep architectures trade interpretability for representation power, and if a use case genuinely needs explainability, that tradeoff should be weighed explicitly rather than defaulting to a deep model simply because it is the current default choice.

For evaluating a vendor claim, the data notes that when a vendor says deep learning, it signals a specific class of neural-network technique, distinct from older, simpler statistical methods still used for many business forecasting tasks, meaning the term is not a synonym for AI in general.

The data does not detail how many layers qualify a network as deep or compare interpretability approaches for deep models. It establishes why deep learning generalized across domains and what it costs in interpretability, not a technical specification.

/ai-glossary/enshittification/.body:
Enshittification is platform decay as a service shifts from serving users to extracting from them, and the data applies it specifically to AI feature bloat wherever assistants are bolted on to raise metrics rather than help.

That AI-specific application is the data's central point, illustrated concretely: a beloved app degrading as mandatory AI features crowd the interface is the data's example of the pattern in a product a user already relied on, the addition of AI features making the product worse for the person using it rather than better.

For reporting on this pattern, the data offers a specific diagnostic question: whether a new AI feature was built to solve a user problem or to move an internal metric, since the data notes the two are often confused in press releases, with a metric-driven feature described in language that suggests it serves the user.

The data frames this as a recognizable and increasingly common pattern in AI feature rollouts specifically, distinct from other product decay dynamics because AI assistants are the vehicle being bolted on. The data does not describe how to distinguish a genuinely user-serving AI feature from one that only appears to be, beyond the metric-versus-problem framing, or quantify how widespread this pattern has become. It establishes the diagnostic question worth asking about a given feature, not a method for auditing a product at scale. The term was coined by Cory Doctorow, 2022.

/ai-glossary/foundation-model/.body:
A foundation model is a large model trained once on broad data at scale and then adapted cheaply for many downstream tasks, an economic logic of amortization where GPT, Claude, and Llama each serve as the base for countless separate products.

That amortization is what makes the enormous upfront cost of training a model like this economically viable across an entire industry built on top of it. Fine-tuning or prompting a foundation model is almost always cheaper and faster than training from scratch, so training from scratch is reserved for cases where the foundation model's pretraining data or architecture genuinely does not fit the target domain.

For anyone evaluating an AI product, the practical implication is that most products bought today are built on someone else's foundation model rather than a custom-trained one, and that is usually the right choice. The useful diagnostic question is whether a vendor's capability comes from the foundation model itself or from what they built on top of it.

This data does not cover how foundation models are trained, what distinguishes one foundation model's capability from another, or the licensing terms that govern building on top of them.

/ai-glossary/godfathers-of-ai/.body:
Godfathers of AI is the informal label for Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Yann LeCun, who shared the 2018 Turing Award for their foundational deep learning work, and the nickname has become sharper since their later public disagreement about AI risk.

The three did share one body of work and one award, but they do not share one view on where AI is headed or how dangerous it is. Headlines contrasting one godfather's warnings with another's optimism are not a rhetorical device, they reflect a genuine and public split among the three people the label groups together.

That gap matters for how the term should be used in coverage or argument. Attributing a single view to the godfathers of AI collectively misrepresents an actual disagreement between specific, named individuals, so citing the group as a unified voice on AI risk does not hold up against what they have each said publicly.

This data does not cover the specific content of each godfather's position on AI risk, or other researchers sometimes included under the same informal label.

/ai-glossary/gradient-descent/.body:
