Style transfer, super-resolution, and early deepfake generation all trace to this architecture, and its central weakness is training instability. Mode collapse and vanishing gradients for the generator are common failure modes inherent to the minimax objective, and that instability motivated much of the theoretical work on alternative generative approaches that eventually led to diffusion-based models.

GANs have been mostly superseded by diffusion models for new image-generation projects because of that training-stability gap, but they retain one real advantage: producing output in a single forward pass rather than many denoising steps gives them a speed edge for real-time or latency-sensitive generation that diffusion models still do not match.

This data does not cover how mode collapse is diagnosed or mitigated, how GAN output quality compares numerically to diffusion output, or specific real-time applications currently using GANs in production.

/ai-glossary/natural-language-understand.body:
Natural language understanding is the subfield focused on extracting meaning and intent from text, as opposed to producing it, and it is what turns "I can't log in" into an actionable support category, shown in practice as intent classification routing tickets in a support system.

This is the comprehension side of the field, distinct from generation: NLU converts an unstructured statement into an actionable, structured category, like authentication issue, that a downstream system or team can route and act on. That conversion step is what makes an unstructured customer complaint usable by anything downstream, whether that is a routing rule, a specialized team, or an automated response.

Generation quality and comprehension quality are separable, though, and worth testing separately. A model can generate fluent, well-written responses while still misclassifying the underlying user intent, which breaks downstream routing logic even though the visible output reads perfectly well, so a support system's quality often depends as much on its NLU accuracy for categorization as on the eventual response it generates.

This data does not cover how intent classification models are trained or evaluated, specific accuracy figures for NLU systems, or how NLU handles ambiguous or multi-intent input.

/ai-glossary/artificial-general-intellig.body:
Artificial General Intelligence is hypothetical AI able to understand, learn, and apply knowledge across any intellectual task at or above human level, and the data's central caution is that the term anchors both investment theses and safety debates despite no agreed test for when it has arrived.

That absence of an agreed test is what the data treats as the practical problem with the term. As an engineering term, it calls AGI nearly useless, since there is no benchmark that constitutes proof of arrival, and recommends technical roadmaps focus on specific, measurable capabilities rather than progress toward an undefined destination. Lab mission statements and policy debates organized around reaching or governing AGI are the data's example of how the term functions in practice, orienting institutions around a goal nobody can verify has been reached.

For evaluating a claim that uses the term, the data recommends real skepticism toward any vendor's AGI timeline specifically because there is no industry-agreed definition, and treats a specific, falsifiable capability claim as more useful for planning than a prediction about AGI arrival.

The data does not offer a working definition more precise than the one given, or describe any proposed test for AGI arrival. It establishes why the term resists technical use and how it functions in investment and safety debates instead, not a resolution to the disagreement. The term was popularized by Ben Goertzel and Shane Legg in the early 2000s.

/ai-glossary/aivss-ai-vulnerability-scor.body:
AIVSS is an OWASP scoring method for rating the severity of AI-specific vulnerabilities, the AI analog of CVSS for conventional software flaws, and the data's point is functional: scores are what turn a pile of findings into a sequenced remediation roadmap.

That sequencing function is the actual value, not the scoring exercise itself. Ranking a prompt-injection exposure against a model-exfiltration risk to decide which gets fixed first is the data's example of what the score is used for, comparing two different kinds of AI-specific vulnerabilities on one consistent scale so a team can prioritize rather than guess or fix findings in whatever order they were discovered.

The data recommends adopting a consistent scoring methodology like this one specifically because a documented, defensible prioritization is what stands up under later scrutiny after an incident, as opposed to triaging AI vulnerabilities by gut feeling. That same structure gives a concrete question to ask a security team: what are the highest-scored open AI vulnerabilities, and what is the remediation timeline for each, rather than a vague assurance that AI security is being worked on.

The data does not detail how AIVSS scores are calculated or what its severity bands are. It establishes what the score is for, sequencing remediation and supporting comparable severity assessment across organizations, not the scoring formula itself. It comes from the OWASP AI Vulnerability Scoring System project.

/ai-glossary/grpo-group-relative-policy-.body:
GRPO is a reinforcement learning method that ranks groups of sampled outputs against each other, removing the separate value model that PPO requires, and DeepSeek's 2024 introduction of it cut the cost of reasoning-model training substantially, with reasoning models now trained on GRPO at a fraction of PPO's compute.

The cost reduction comes directly from what the method removes. A separate value model, the component PPO needs to score how good an output is, adds real training cost and complexity of its own. Comparing a group of sampled attempts against each other and rewarding the relatively better ones sidesteps that requirement entirely, which is a genuinely simpler engineering pattern than classical PPO-based reinforcement learning from human feedback.

That simplicity is part of why GRPO sits behind many current reasoning-model releases specifically, since reasoning-focused training runs at a scale where the compute savings from dropping a value model compound significantly. The open question is how the stability and sample-efficiency tradeoffs of group-relative comparison compare to a learned value function baseline across different task domains, which remains an active comparison point in current research.

This data does not cover the mathematical mechanics of group-relative ranking, specific compute savings figures, or how GRPO performs outside reasoning-model training.

/ai-glossary/cosais-control-overlays-for.body:
COSAiS is a NIST project mapping the SP 800-53 control catalog onto AI systems, and the data locates it precisely relative to another framework: the implementation detail beneath the Cyber AI Profile, where the profile says what outcomes matter, the overlays say which controls produce them.

That division of labor is the practical point. Selecting the overlay controls for a generative AI deployment instead of hand-picking from 800-53 is the data's example of using the mapping directly, applying an existing, structured interpretation rather than independently reinventing an AI-specific reading of each control from the general catalog. The recommendation for a security team implementing 800-53-based controls for an AI system is to use this mapping directly rather than building a parallel interpretation from scratch.

For consistency across organizations, the data frames a structured mapping of a widely recognized control catalog onto AI-specific guidance as supporting more consistent security control implementation and assessment, reducing ambiguity in how conventional security frameworks apply to AI systems specifically.

The data does not list which specific 800-53 controls are covered by the overlays or describe how the mapping was developed. It establishes the overlay's relationship to the Cyber AI Profile and its practical use, not the content of the mapping itself. It comes from the NIST Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems project.

/ai-glossary/reinforcement-learning-with.body:
RLVR is reinforcement learning where the reward comes from an objective checker, a test suite or answer key, rather than human preference, and it removed the preference bottleneck for domains with ground truth, and it is how modern reasoning models train, seen in math answers and unit tests grading millions of attempts automatically.

That removal of the bottleneck is the direct mechanism behind its impact. Human preference labeling is slow, expensive, and inherently limited in volume, but domains with an objective, checkable answer, code passing tests, math problems with known solutions, can scale training reward signal far beyond what human labeling alone could support, since a test suite can grade attempts automatically at a volume no team of human raters could match.

That reliance on checkable ground truth also explains where the technique's gains concentrate and where they do not. RLVR works best precisely where ground truth is checkable, which is why its biggest gains show up in domains like code and math rather than open-ended writing, where correctness is not a binary automatic check the way a passing test or a correct numerical answer is. Extending verifiable-reward training beyond these narrow, clean domains into broader reasoning and real-world tasks where correctness is harder to automatically verify is a central and actively pursued research direction right now, not a solved extension.

This data does not cover how RLVR reward signals are technically constructed, how verifiable rewards compare quantitatively to RLHF on the same tasks, or what current research approaches to extending verifiability look like.
